subsubtopic: MAIL ORDER SALES IN UNITED STATES-INVESTIGATION REQUESTED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, they should have called it the "great Canadian lottery rip-off' but instead it is labelled "your official Canadian lottery form". What is it? It is an invitation to participate in the official Canadian Government lottery and win up to $50 million in cash. It is described as just like playing keno in Las Vegas, and is the lure to rip off thousands of Americans who have been purchasing these tickets from at least four Canadian mail order companies at mark-ups of almost up to 400 per cent.
In fact this official form has so flooded the market that, on a recent visit that I made to the State of Florida, three of my husband's relatives had received this unsolicited pitch in the mail. Not only was there a promise of million dollar winners, the so-called official guarantee said that one in four had a chance to win.
We know that the Ontario Government is already acting to prohibit mail order sales outside the province. However, we also know that at least one agent buys his tickets outside the province anyway so that the action of the Ontario Government alone will not stop this rip-off.
1 ask the federal Government to launch an immediate investigation into mail fraud and false advertising, and further ask the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) to include in his Criminal Code amendments a provision to ensure this fly-bynight operation is illegal across Canada.
The Government talks about our great friendship with the United States. Now is the chance to put this claim into practice by preventing the wholesale rip-off of our American neighbours and consumers.

Mr. Speaker, only one day of debate is left before the Government will impose on Canadians Bill C-70, an Act to reduce the deficit at
the expense of the poor and children. Closure was imposed on a debate and the Government has reduced indexation of January family allowance cheques even before the legislation has passed.
It sought advice from the public and from experts, and then ignored it. This farcical consultation process has alienated organizations representing most Canadians, including women s organizations, poor people's organizations, social policy groups, labour, church groups and many more. Experts stated unanimously that deindexation of the family allowance below the rate of inflation will be harmful to children, families, and the poor. The Conservative Government has ignored their testimony and their research.
Now New Brunswick has added its voice to the growing list of protestors. A spokesperson states:
We view this proposed cut-back as one further piece of evidence of the disregard and contempt that the federal Government holds toward this Maritime province, especially in view of the following facts: 35 per cent of New Brunswick's children live in poverty; 43 per cent of rural children live in poverty and 47 per cent of the 64,000 people on social assistance are children. What good will the federal Government's cut-backs to child benefits do for these children?
Petitions continue to flow from all parts of Canada-

Mail service is a line of communication binding our peoples together. It is the lifeblood of commerce and industry. That is why we want, need, and deserve a model, first-class postal service and we on this side of the House will not be happy until we have one.
The importance of the system is no more evident than it is at Christmas, and this year postal workers and retirees brought Christmas to many homes throughout southwestern Ontario.
Sixty thousand letters addressed to Santa Claus were answered. Schools in St. Catharines, for instance, competed for window space, resulting in a cheerful, colorful atmosphere to work in and to visit.
Many offices placed Christmas trees in their lobbies to have customers and employees contribute gifts for distribution by the Salvation Army and associated charities.
Literally hundreds of post office employees were involved in this voluntary effort at a time when the Post Office was handling a higher than usual volume of mail and, for the most part, pleasantly and on time.
Now if we could have that attitude and commitment to service through the 365 days of the year, we would all be proud to sing out: "Canada Post: It's Ours".

Mr. Speaker, the current security alert at Ottawa, Toronto, and Montreal airports is an unfortunate fact of life in today's climate of international terrorism. No country is immune from the insanity of terrorism, not even Canada. Each country must develop its own master plan or strategic response to every aspect of the terrorist menace, from security searches and precautions through to informing the public of the specific nature of a threat.
The manner in which information on the airport threats was supplied to the public in the last 36 hours leaves a lot to be desired. Even though the stepped-up security was obvious at the airports in question, information to the public was coming
out piecemeal at best. Fear, uncertainty, and rumours thrive in this sort of an atmosphere to the detriment of airport workers, the travelling public, and concerned citizens.
I would submit, Mr. Speaker, that the public has a right to know the level of risk involved where a terrorist threat is present, and the Government has a duty to furnish prompt information to the public. The Government should be more forthright so that Canadians have enough information to be able to make up their own minds on whether to travel by air or to stay home.

subtopic: INCREASED DRILLING ACTIVITY-BEAUFORT SEA OIL DISCOVERY
INCREASED DRILLING ACTIVITY-BEAUFORT SEA OIL DISCOVERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, drilling for minerals and fossil fuels in Canada reached a record high in recent months. Currently there is not a diamond drill available for hire east of the Manitoba border, thanks to the flow-through share initiatives put in place by the Government.
In addition, some 11,720 oil or gas wells were drilled in the four western provinces in 1985.
Quietly, a few days ago, perhaps the most dramatic drilling news in recent years was announced when the test results on the Amauligak 1-65 well in the Beaufort Sea became known. The flow rates and calculated production capability are among the highest recorded in Canada. Oil flowed at rates of more than 7,000 barrels per day from two intervals, with calculated production capacity at one of the intervals at almost 35,000 barrels per day.
The result of the 1-65 well indicated the Amauligak structure contains at least 400 million barrels of oil, and reserves could be as high as 900 million barrels. With total reserves in the near and offshore in the Beaufort now reaching a billion barrels, production is a real possibility. By comparison, reserves in Hibernia are estimated to be between 500 million and 800 million barrels.
This means that we are closer to energy self-sufficiency. It means new jobs. It means new wealth. It is another dimension to our national sovereignty. The Government has created an encouraging economic environment for risk ventures. The oil industry-

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. La Salle) intends to continue with the lay-offs of some 270 cleaners who work in post offices across Canada. Many of these people are longterm employees close to retirement; a couple of dozen are within a year of retirement. Many of them are disabled. Only six of these people have found alternative work, and not one of them has been retrained.
The fact is that these employees will be replaced by a private contractor, so the Government will still have to pay for the service. The Public Works policy of contracting out is based upon outdated information. It will cost almost as much in welfare, unemployment insurance and forgone income taxes to keep these people unemployed.
How can the Minister justify these particular lay-offs? Even if the Minister's own standards of behaviour condone the laying-off of people and their replacement by others, does he not realize that most Canadians disagree with his actions? In fact, 61 per cent of Canadians polled on this issue find his actions unacceptable, and only a small minority support his actions. Does the Minister think that he is some little northern Ronald Reagan taking on a great and powerful union and crushing them. Wake up, Mr. Minister. These are some of the lowest paid people doing essential work. Most Canadians find the Minister's actions repugnant, wasteful, and unacceptable.

According to a recent survey carried out by the Conseil du patronat du Quebec, Mr. Speaker, business people are anticipating a continuation of the economic recovery the beginning of which coincided with the election of a Progressive Conservative Government in Ottawa. In the province of Quebec, Mr. Speaker, 73 per cent of all businessmen and women interviewed stated that they were optimistic as to the economic future in their province. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, three of every four persons surveyed expressed the opinion that the current political climate was good; 73 per cent of them felt that this climate, likely to favour investment and job creation, would continue to improve over the next few months.
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that the new climate of consultation and co-operation with the provinces, including Quebec, has contributed to this very positive assessment of the economic outlook for Quebec. Also, the leadership demonstrated by our Government in the area of job creation and economic expertise could only contribute to this most positive assessment of our economic outlook. Mr. Speaker, such optimism

Mr. Speaker, during yesterday's Question Period the Government demonstrated the regressive and "look at the past" attitude which has shamefully characterized its handling of the Japanese Canadian redress issue.
During his days as Opposition Leader and throughout the 1984 campaign, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) spoke of the need to settle this issue quickly. However, once in office, not only did his commitments quickly dissolve, but he refused to meet or acknowledge the National Association of Japanese Canadians. To make matters worse, his former Multicultural-ism Minister abruptly cut off talks with the association and attempted to proceed unilaterally. Now the present Minister refuses to honour his promise to negotiate, preferring instead to play up the differences which exist in any national issue. All these manoeuvres border on moral dishonesty.
We often criticize the United States on the question of minority rights. However, on the issue of redress 1 urge the Prime Minister to weigh the steps being launched in the U.S., to recall the promises he made, to consider his failure to live up to these expectations, and then to ask himself if his actions have been fair, honorable, and courageous.
This matter requires more sensitivity and seriousness rather than simply issuing a Prime Minister's Office press release stating that Mila Mulroney will be visiting the ethnocultural communities. We need action, and we need it now.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak today on Bill C-84, an Act to amend the Income Tax Act and several related statutes. These include the Canada Pension Plan, the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, the Financial Administration Act and the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Act.
The Bill contains measures proposed in two notices of ways and means motions tabled in the House earlier this year, one being a general way and means motion tabled on May 23 and the other being a detailed notice of ways and means motion tabled on November 21.
The Bill represents a substantial and integral component of the Government's program to secure durable economic renewal for Canadians. Hon. Member will recall that we established the broad framework for that strategy in November, 1984. Since then we have moved clearly and consistently to develop and to implement specific initiatives which are the building blocks for durable economic growth.

January 17, 1986
Income Tax Act, 1986

This Bill is an important component of the program developed by this Government to ensure a lasting economic renewal for all Canadians. Hon. Members will recall that we outlined that strategy in November 1984. Since then, we have acted clearly and continuously to develop and implement special measures which have contributed to a lasting economic renewal.

The renewal strategy is designed to create steady and sustained improvement in the basic conditions for economic growth.
The Bill proposes to continue our strategy for far-reaching and wide-ranging economic renewal. Therefore, it is appropriate to review briefly the corner-stones of that strategy. First, the Government is determined to reduce the federal deficit and bring the growth of the public debt under control. A second corner-stone of the renewal strategy is the direct encouragement of private initiative as the key to productive growth and job creation. Third, we are improving the efficiency and effectiveness of Government by cutting waste, by removing obstacles to economic growth and by making better use of scarce and precious resources. We are ensuring that Government assumes a less instrusive place in the lives of Canadians.
Finally, we are bringing about all these vital changes in a manner which is as fair as humanly possible. In acting to improve the climate in which our private sector in Canada can excel, we are building on the basic senses of compassion, tolerance and justice, which are the essence and the character of our Canadian society.
The Bill we are considering today is firmly and squarely based on these corner-stones of the economic renewal strategy. The Bill will implement many significant measures which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) introduced in the Government's first full Budget. These measures have attracted widespread support and are eagerly awaited by Canadians. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, this Bill contains very important amendments to the Income Tax Act. If I may, I would like to mention some of them.
First, there is the $500,000 capital gains exemption. As I have already said in this House, this amendment will change the attitude of Canadians as far as savings and investment are concerned and help the whole business sector, especially small businessmen.
Mr. Speaker, when I speak about small businessmen, this includes the farmers. They own small businesses, and after meeting farmers in my constituency, whether they are from Yamachiche, Saint-Barnabe, Saint-Severe or Pointe-du-Lac, I know that they are impatient for the Budget to come into effect, especially the $500,000 lifetime capital gains exemption.
Mr. Speaker, a second important point is the provisions that investments in pension plans and RRSPs may now be used for small businesses.
Mr. Speaker, as you know, this Bill will allow all those who have RRSPs or RRSFs to use this money to purchase equity in our small businesses, which will help these businesses to expand and provide a new source of capital, which is essential to develop our economy and create more jobs.
A third part of Bill C-84 concerns the income-splitting provisions which used to provide a means to avoid paying taxes for members of the same family. We all know that, very often, there were interest-free loans between members of a same family and the person who had no income at that time declared interest income on which very little or no taxes were payable. Bill C-84 eliminates this loophole.
Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that the Opposition has not pointed out that this is a good thing. We have not heard about it from the other side and I think that if the Oppostion had been honest, they would have applauded this initiative.
The fourth change concerns the administration of the taxation system. Seizures and all search activities carried out under the previous system by the Department of Revenue, which had been mentioned frequently under the former Government, have been eliminated.
A fifth measure proposed in the Budget was the risk capital fund for workers. Individuals who invest in risk capital funds constituted by workers will now be entitled to a tax credit amounting to 20 per cent of the cost of purchase. This is another very useful measure which unfortunately has not been mentioned very often by the Opposition.
Mr. Speaker, the sixth point concerns research and development. Tax credits for small businesses up to $2 million will provide a 100 per cent refund instead of 40 per cent as is the case now.
All those are positive measures, Mr. Speaker. 1 could go on for a long time, but I think that, after reading Bill C-84, it is easy to see that this legislation is of vital importance for the Canadian economy and for all Canadians.
In conclusion, this Bill provides for a new direction for the Canadian income tax system, new measures such as the $500,000 lifetime personal capital gains exemption to encourage Canadians to invest their savings in productivity of Canadian activity and to take business risks.
This Bill improves the fairness of the tax system by removing some of the ways in which unintended advantage may be taken of the tax system and increases the effectiveness of government programs by reducing the base for investment tax credit where other grants or assistance have been received for expenditures made.
January 17, 1986

This Bill increases the fairness of the tax system by introducing change of control rules to prevent unacceptable sales of unused tax credits. These changes are long overdue. We know that Canadians share our desire to improve the economy and are willing to share the burdens so that we will all share the triumphs.
This is a major Bill. It is in some areas complex, but such complexity is unavoidable where measures such as those contained in this Bill affect the fundamental principles of our tax system. The new direction this Bill provides, and the benefits that Canadians will gain more than justify the changes. Mr. Speaker, 1 recommend Bill C-84 to this House, and I look forward to the speedy passage of these measures.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext: In the context 1 think we will waive the technical issue of a question and comment period. Therefore, 1 give the floor now to the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner).

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
The
Parliamentary Secretary has just urged a speedy passage. The House Leader has taken care of that by imposing closure on the Bill. 1 cannot remember, in major pieces of legislation reflecting what is at the core of the Government's economic philosophy of budget where closure has been applied in this type of case, where the debate has been limited in the House of Commons, and where the committee hearings have been restrained to one week's hearings.
That gets to the issue that troubled the House earlier today in Question Period when the Government-in return for getting an agreement on how this Bill was to be treated, among others-made an undertaking before Christmas to open up committee hearings on the de Havilland affair.
True, Your Honour referred to those matters as being committee proceedings, but the issue related to an order of the House which limited the time available for debate, of course, reinforced unilaterally by the Government using the hammer of closure.
It is with no disrespect to the Parliamentary Secretary that I suggest to him and to the Government that on the third reading of a budget Bill reflecting the economic policy of the Government the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) should be in the House, and so should the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall). I had the honour of holding that portfolio, the Ministry of Finance, for four years and I always made it a practice as Minister to attend to Bills personally in the House of Commons, not always during the report stage, but certainly during the second reading and third reading stages of a major piece of legislation. I consider it to be a continuing affront to the House, and I say that with respect, Your Honour, that Ministers are disregarding that courtesy and not attending the House when their legislation is being considered.
I want to congratulate our financial critic, the Member of Parliament for Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston), ably supported by the Member of Parliament for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) and the Member of Parliament for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) who have had the custody on our
Income Tax Act, 1986
side for the disposition of this Bill and for the critique of the Bill. I want to state what I stated during the budget debate. We have grave concerns about the tenor, tone and substance of this Bill. We thinks it reflects a Budget that is unfair. We think it reflects a Budget that is sneaky. We think it reflects a Budget that is unnecessarily taking money out of the economy, particularly the domestic economy, to the detriment of Canadian owned small business. This Government enjoys the largest majority in Canadian history. It has also presented to the Canadian people in this Budget the largest tax increase in Canadian history. Instead of the Minister of Finance having the courage and the guts to stand up on budget afternoon and say to Canadians, "I am raising your taxes", he did it in a sneaky, clandestine and hidden fashion. Most of the tax increase is done at the sales tax level and at the deindexing level.
I had the honour in 1972, unanimously supported by the Conservative Party at the time, of indexing our taxes, that is to say I indexed the brackets and the deductions to reflect the erosion of inflation on the income of Canadians. I did it with the unanimous support of the country and of the Leader of the Opposition at the time, Mr. Robert Stanfield. We did it because we felt it unfair that Canadians should be taxed at higher rates because of the inter-reaction of inflation against the progressive tax system. They may have received salary increases, but when you balanced that against inflation there was no real increase at all. There might have been a nominal increase in their salary or their wage rate, but no real increase at all. Yet by moving them into higher tax brackets the Ministry of Finance took that money from them.
Because of this hidden tax we have not only a sneakiness in the system, because the Minister did not have the guts to say he was going to tax Canadians by an increase of 3 per cent per year, per year, he just deindexed the system by 3 per cent per year, per year, but the way that the deindexing is going to work will have very unfair consequences. Not only is it hidden, but it will hit the lowest income earners hardest.
I recite figures that my colleague, the Member of Parliament for Laval-des-Rapides got from an official document from the Department of Finance which was never denied by the Minister as not being legitimate. We get these figures over a period of four consecutive years cumulative. A man or a woman in this country earning $15,000 a year will have a cumulative tax increase in four years of 36 per cent. A man or a woman earning $30,000 a year will have a cumulative four-year increase of only 11 per cent, compared to that 36 per cent. If you earn $100,000 a year in this country over that four-year period, your cumulative tax increase will be 4 per cent. If you happen to earn $200,000, that cumulative tax increase over the same period of time will only be 2 per cent- $15,000 a year, a 36 per cent increase, $200,000 a year, a 2 per cent increase. Now, that is not fair and it is not perceived by the Canadian people to be fair. When you take that and couple it with the capital gains tax exemption of $500,000 over a lifetime, reduced at the maximum rate to a $125,000 cash

January 17, 1986
Income Tax Act, 1986
bonanza, you have inequity taken, I believe, to a Dranconian degree.
The average family is taxed about $450 to $500 a year more. Over a period of four years, there is a cumulative tax increase of 30 per cent to 36 per cent. Yet when you add back that capital gains tax exemption to the wealthier, the man or woman earning $200,000 a year will be 4 per cent or 5 per cent ahead. Only 4 per cent of the earners in this country invest in a way that will make them eligible for that tax bonanza.
So I am saying that we have had here a real revelation of a Tory philosophy. After nine months of cosmetic politics, of a meeting with the President of the United States on St. Patrick's Day, and on Valentine's Day a meeting with the provincial premiers in Regina, then a national economic conference, and all the cosmetics and photo opportunities that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) loves so well, he finally came up with a Budget. It has been the longest period of time in modern Canadian history between an election and a Budget. All the deductions, all the tax brackets are being deindexed by 3 per cent a year, and that will mean, in gross terms, by 1989 a hidden tax increase over what we have now of $11.5 billion. The Minister of Finance did not have the courage, the guts, the frankness or the forthrightness to stand up in this House before Your Honour and admit that.
Mr. Speaker, when the Government tried to de-index Old Age Security pensions, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) had the audacity to claim before the House that he had the support of our Canadian senior citizens. He was badly mistaken. Finally, after thousands and thousands of petitions and signatures were tabled in the House, after public meetings were held across this country, 2.5 million pensioners protested because they felt deceived and betrayed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Government of Canada, and because the Prime Minister had made a commitment in Sherbrooke, during the election campaign, when he said to all our senior citizens: I am protecting you against inflation and I will never withdraw that protection. In the Budget, that protection was reduced by three per cent annually. Finally, justice prevailed thanks to the people of Canada, the unions, and even businessmen and women, and all the organizations.
We were frankly disgusted, and that is putting it mildly, at the lack of understanding and the insensitivity of this Government.
This Government, which had shown itself to be entirely devoid of compassion, fortunately was not able to execute its plan. Nevertheless, this Bill, as I said before, is widening the gap between rich and poor in Canada.

Let me outline for Your Honour, the House and the country the impact on the disposable income of families of all the
budget measures, most of which are contained in this Bill. I am talking now about the immediate effect of the budget measures, not the cumulative effect that I recited earlier. A family with an income of $15,000 per year will have $634 less in disposable income as a result of the budget measures. That is 9.8 per cent less. A family with an income of $20,000 per year will have a disposable income of $808 less as a result of this Budget or 8.5 per cent less. A family earning $30,000 per year will have $1,089 or 7.9 per cent less. A family earning $40,000 per year will have a disposable income of $359 or 1.9 per cent less.
Because of the cumulative effect of this Budget, a family earning up to $75,000 per year will have a disposable income of $1,269 or 3.3 per cent more. The disposable income of a family earning $100,000 per year will increase by $2,054 or 3.9 per cent. A family earning $200,000 per year will have $4,519 or 4.2 per cent more. Is that fair? Is that what the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister consider to be a fair sharing of the burden of getting the public finances under control? If that is so, I think they have been blindly misled and I believe the people of the country will have a reckoning sooner than they think.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-West-mount, spoke eloquently on the $500,000 capital gains tax exemption. As you know, Mr. Speaker, we presented two amendments to the House on that issue. Sixty-three per cent of that benefit will go to 4 per cent of the taxpayers of the country. The rather feeble rationale that the Minsiter of Finance attempted to give for this measure was that it would encourage investment and jobs, but there is nothing in the measure before the House to limit that bonanza to Canadian-owned businesses. There is nothing in the measure to limit it to companies registered or listed on Canadian stock exchanges. It is wide open.
The capital gains tax exemption can be benefited from whether one invests in a condominium in Florida, an apartment building in Hong Kong or European art. There is nothing to relate the exemption to Canadian production, jobs and growth, and that was the reason my colleague, the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount, introduced an amendment designed to give a tax break on Canadian investments only. I might say that although members of the NDP voted against that particular amendment, they introduced it in committee. They thought it made good sense then and it does make good sense now.
I do not agree with the capital gains tax exemption at all. I do not think it should have been introduced in this Budget. I do not think the Government can give a bonanza of $125,000 to the rich and wealthy and those fortunate enough to be able to invest in assets while taxing the average Canadian family the way it has been taxed under this Budget. However, if there is going to be a tax exemption, it should at least be limited to Canadian investments, companies and businesses.
The only excuse that the Minister gave for not limiting this tax exemption to Canadian investments was that it would make the tax system too complex. As my colleague, the Hon.
January 17, 1986

Member for Laval-des-Rapides, pointed out, even those who would benefit from this cash bonanza, reinforced by tax lawyers and tax accountants, recognize that the way this exemption has been constructed, when combined with the minimum tax proposal, it will lever investment in favour of offshore and American markets rather than the Canadian market. What these measures do to tax dividends means that it is now more useful for those with surplus funds to invest in the American market and benefit from a lower tax rate than qualify for Canadian dividends from Canadian companies. The Minister has a hopeless situation on his hands. He is encouraging investment outside the country by the interlocking of these two measures.
When talking about a complex income tax system let me point out that those who live in Quebec have to deal with four tax codes. There is the Quebec tax code, the federal Income Tax Act which this Bill is purportedly amending, the new minimum tax code, and the capital gains tax exemption code. It is impossible for the average person to understand how this system was put together. The Minister has not simplified or reformed the system. He has added layer upon layer of complexity, which will only discourage investment and, as I have said, encourage those with the power to invest to go beyond our shores.

In the House and in committee, my colleagues have already mentioned the fact that this Bill also puts an end to the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan. For eleven years, more than 2.5 million Canadians have been using this plan to help buy their first home. Many young couples have taken advantage of this mechanism to acquire their own home as soon as they started a family. To them it meant recognition of the fact that Canadians and especially young Canadians see owning their own homes as a right. Today, however, the obstacles facing young people in this respect are almost insurmountable, and despite our efforts and a number of amendments that were tabled in the House, the Government has withdrawn the RHOSP. To quote my colleague from Mont-real-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart), this Government is very "mal runne", and I could not agree more.

When the Minister introduced the Budget, he said that he wanted to get the deficit under control. A set up question was asked of him this morning so that he could try to indicate to the country that he was on his own target. We will see. Whatever he has done, he has done on the backs of the unemployed and on the backs of middle-class families.
Both in response to the question this morning and in response to the question I put to the Minister on Tuesday when I asked where the Canadian dollar is going and if the Minister will admit that higher interest rates are being provoked by the Governor of the Bank of Canada in order to stabilize or prop up our dollar, the Minister was trying to patch things up. In response to my question, he was forced to tell me to wait for his February Budget. That was a recognition by the Minister
Income Tax Act, 1986
that the real reason the dollar is falling and has been in speculative trouble is that there has been a lack of confidence on world markets that this country is being properly run. The Minister was forced to say that in the House on Tuesday, and he had a set up question asked of him to try to indicate to the markets that he was on target today. That displays an anxiety on the part of the Minister who is trying to reassure the markets so that the Bank of Canada will not have to inject more funds into the system in order to prop up a falling currency.
We believe that the tax Bill before the House also reflects lousy economics. It takes billions of dollars out of the economy. It reflects a Government that is relying primarily on the export thrust to maintain the health of the Canadian economy. Most of the purchasing power that will be drawn out by this Budget, $11.5 billion in four years, will be to the detriment of small Canadian independent businesses.
When the people of this country voted for this Government, they voted for change. They wanted a new direction. They have not received it. All they have received is incompetence. However, in the Bill which is before us they have received worse than that. In this Bill they see a demonstration of a lack of sensitivity and a demonstration of unfairness. They see a demonstration of the lack of courage of the Minister of Finance and of the Prime Minister who have failed to come clean with respect to the hidden tax increases which are really represented in the Budget.
In terms of the sales tax increases and deindexation of the system, the Canadian people are being hit harder in this Budget than they have been in any Budget tabled in the history of the country. They have been hit in such a way that they will not know what they are being hit with until it creeps up and hits them like a rabbit punch on the back of the neck.
We believe the Budget portrays an insensitivity which does not deserve the confidence of the House. We will not be able to hold it up or stop it. We have been able to say that the Budget reflects an old-fashioned Tory philosophy which says, as the Minister has said: "Sure, you want to encourage those who succeed". However, it certainly does not protect those who are struggling in the country. It does not protect those with families, those who are trying to get above the poverty line, and those who are trying to get ahead. It does not protect those who are trying to build up capital. The Budget reflects old-fashioned market forces which put heat on ordinary Canadians and leave all the scope with those who are able to take care of themselves.
We urge the House not to support this measure. We have done what we could within the limited time given to us under the rules. We have been restrained in what I believe to be a very undemocratic way by the use of closure on a tax Bill. After all, the fundamental role of Parliament is to review the tax system. The fundamental role of Parliament is to review spending. These roles have come down from Westminster. They came about as a result of the early fights between the

January 17, 1986
Income Tax Act, 1986
nobles and the king, fights between the British aristocracy and the Crown, and, eventually, fights between the people and the aristocracy. What Parliament could always refuse was spending. What it could always refuse was the imposition of taxes. There is nothing more important to our system than that there be proper debate and proper scrutiny of these types of measures. Yet, the debate on this measure was restrained. It was curtailed at both the committee stage and before the House.
We oppose this measure. We are revolted by it. We think that it is wrong, unfair and sneaky. We leave it in the hands of the country until we next have an opportunity to deal with it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Roch La Salle (Minister of Public Works):
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner). Obviously this legislation will have a significant impact on all Canadians. Mr. Speaker, I sat on Opposition benches long enough to know that it is a lot easier to make unflattering remarks about a Government which is accountable and assumes its responsibilities. Still I entertain some reservations about the comments of the Leader of the Opposition, for his credibility can be challenged since he too assumed major responsibilities as Minister of Finance in the Government which Canadians turfed right out over twelve months ago.
I vividly recall that the present Leader of the Opposition once decided to return to the private sector rather than stand up for his Party and his Government, as he should have done-

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext: You too decided to join the Union nationale.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Yes, to continue to serve the Quebec voters for whom I have always had consideration and respect.
At least I had the courage to offer my modest contribution to the people of Quebec, I had that kind of courage, unlike the present Leader of the Opposition who chose-as was his right, and I am not criticizing his decision-to look after his own
interests and leave Canadians at the mercy of a Government which was already running out of breath, the same Government to which we owe our current difficulties.
Mr. Speaker, there has to be a limit to such attacks in the House, intended as they are to make Canadians believe that everything we do is wrong, and sometimes in terms which border on demagoguery.
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that changes have to be made, and that is what we are doing because we know where we are going, we know what we want, and we know what Canadians expect from us.
Mr. Speaker, would anybody in his right mind miss this opportunity to remind Canadians that the present Leader of the Opposition heads the Party which is trying to tell us how to improve the management of public affairs and which, as it happened, was in office for the past 15 years when 100,000 more Canadians swelled the ranks of the unemployed year in and year out, at least 1.5 million of them all told? That within our first 15 or 18 months in office we successfully reversed this vicious trend so harmful to Canadians? The judgment rendered by Canadians 15 or 16 months ago already was unmistakable: they simply had had enough of a Government which was driving Canada into bankruptcy. Thank God, our economic performance in recent years indicates quite clearly that things are a lot better than they used to be.
Most business people endowed with a good business sense- some Hon. Members opposite know business very well, much better than I do, Mr. Speaker-realize that the economic performance of this Government is quite encouraging and would deserve much better support than it has received so far.
But Canadians should be aware that Members of the Opposition have a part to play, but only to the extent that the interests if their own constituents are well served.
Mr. Speaker, they will interrupt us, level all sorts of accusations against us and use all means at their disposal to try to hinder the normal operation of Parliament. And they will refuse to help the Government which, through its measures, is trying to restore an economic climate likely to attract investments. But we are on the right track, Mr. Speaker, and well on the way to achieving this objective of a new economic outlook for Canadians. We have a lot of catching up to do. While trying to solve almost hopeless problems, we are being asked to work miracles.
Mr. Speaker, it is not easy to turn the country around and off the direction which was leading Canada to bankruptcy. But we came up with changes and economic policies more than a year ago, and we are glad we did, for we have put an end to this disastrous habit of creating 100,000 new unemployed each year. Instead, as we had hoped and encouraged it to do, the private sector has created between 400,000 and 500,000 new jobs in Canada this year.
January 17, 1986

In Quebec, a province of which I am very fond for readily understandable reasons, we have also managed to put an end to this tragedy and to create over 100,000 jobs. Members of the Opposition will say that it is not enough. They will add that a very serious problem exists in Montreal East.
Mr. Speaker, it is a fact that the previous government's ill-advised policies and lack of long term strategy for Montreal East as well as the rest of Canada have created enormous difficulties, but we have already shown our determination and we have already achieved results which, in the eyes of most businessmen and people of good faith, deserve consideration. And we intend to continue, Mr. Speaker.
The Leader of the Opposition says that the purpose of all our efforts is to help the rich, Mr. Speaker. It is a fact that we have come up with incentives to convince those who can invest to invest even more. I think it makes sense to help them invest more for the purpose of creating new jobs. That is the whole idea. Members opposite know it. Do not think that I am not well aware of the problems experienced by those who are unemployed or on welfare. But it must be realized that they are not in a position to generate new investments tomorrow morning. We must therefore look to people who can. And they are not all millionaires, Mr. Speaker. Quite the contrary. Members opposite are quick to blame the elimination of the capital gains tax, implying again that this action will benefit only a handful of millionaires. But nothing could be farther from the truth. Canadians by the millions will benefit from this action. We need only ask farmers, a class of Canadian citizens which I hold in very high esteem. Farmers are businessmen. Go and ask them whether they feel that this action is not quite in order and encouraging for them. But they are not millionaires. That is not true.
Again, there is a consequence which we have seen and which all members in good faith could see if they wanted. That measure will thus enable farmers to pass their farms on to their children at much less cost, due to the fact that we are allowing them very legitimate profits by way of the proposal called the capital gains tax repeal, Mr. Speaker.
The Leader of the Opposition has also said we lacked interest and respect for mothers because we propose changes to the family allowances. Anyone who is honest and who correctly understands the proposal put forward by my colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), will see it is aimed at something that any man and woman in his or her right mind would support, and that is helping the most in need, Mr. Speaker. And by rationalizing the child tax credit and the dependent child benefit and family allowances, we are indeed increasing our assistance to mothers or families most in need, those whose income is considered low.
Mr. Speaker, it is clear in all those instances that this new concept permeating our Government is aimed indeed above all
Income Tax Act, 1986
at reviving the Canadian economy, which in my view is the first responsibility of a Government, restoring hope to those young Canadians who were facing unbelievable despair because of an unemployment rate that was so prejudicial to the whole Canadian nation.
Therefore, during the past fifteen months, Mr. Speaker, interest rates have come down in a way that is both significant and encouraging for the construction industry. Thousands of jobs have been created in the construction industry, and also jobs related to the building of thousands of new homes. The inflation rate has been maintained at a much more encouraging level than that experienced over the last five or ten years. Economic growth has taken place and surprisingly, at a still higher rate than was experienced in the United States. Business confidence also increased, and this is important when we want to give the private sector all due credit in that economic renewal. And we do have confidence in the private sector. However, and I was forgetting this, they are blaming us because of this legislation repealing tax credits, capital gains tax, because we had made no provision for dictating to Canadians where they should invest those capital gains.
Contrary to what that Government did for so many years, we will not dictate to Canadians how they will live, not even in their kitchens. We have confidence in Canadians, and in forthcoming measures all those who can invest will also find incentives to invest those gains within the Canadian economy. We do not believe that Canadians will hastily send abroad the savings or gains they may have realized within our Canadian economy that is equally respectful of all Canadians, in order to favour foreign economies. Quite the opposite, Mr. Speaker, we do a lot of thinking. Our first reaction is to trust the Canadian people as a whole.
Today we appreciate the competence Canadians are showing and already, Mr. Speaker, we are assured that those Canadians who have the means will invest their money in Canadian industries because also of the benefits we will offer them. Why? We always have in mind creating jobs in all areas as sophisticated as those of new technology.
That is the goal of the Government we represent, for which 1 think I have every reason to ask the support of all Hon. Members, to recapture the wealth which the previous Government woefully squandered. And to redistribute fairly to all Canadians the money they pay in taxes, we must rebuild the wealth we have lost, and we have a wonderful opportunity to do so by means of measures which also convey the interest of all those investors who also wish to contribute to the building of this country in all generosity and fairness to our whole nation. I am therefore unimpressed by the attack that was launched today by the Leader of the Opposition who stooped so low as to comment only in negative terms on our economic performance which is envied by many countries around the world.

January 17, 1986
Income Tax Act, 1986
I owe thanks, of course, to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), my colleagues in the Cabinet and all Members of our party who accepted and approved the sort of measures we are proposing. True, Mr. Speaker, we still have a lot to do. But we have nonetheless succeeded, in a short time, in clearing the atmosphere with the provinces. We have also assured them that they will play a greater role in the momentous decisions the Canadian Government will have to take. The Members opposite will go on voicing their pessimistic views and will do all they can to have Canadians believe we are on the wrong track. However, the facts speak for themselves. Canadians will see through the rhetoric, they will understand the meaning of this opposition, the reasons behind this negative attitude and this desire to misinform the public.
These people, Mr. Speaker-and Canadians must be aware of it-do not want us to achieve this urgent economic recovery which is already under way. These people, and the Leader of the Official Opposition in particular, know perfectly well that if we succeed, even in limited way, they will never regain power with the limited team they have. They are missing the opportunity to abide by their commitments to the voters, Mr. Speaker. It is disheartening for all Canadians, Mr. Speaker, to see that these people refuse to assume their fundamental responsability: representing the legitimate interests of their constituents, which in this case means ensuring economic recovery, a quick recovery in all parts of Canada, not only in Quebec, through investment and hard work. To this end, Mr. Speaker, we are forced to ask Canadians to make sacrifices, we must ask them to help pay for a $200 billion national debt, incurred by our friends opposite. We wonder whether Canadians agreed with this approach that created an artificial economy which, today, has become a terrible burden for the entire country, and to what extent the present Leader of the Opposition and Opposition Members are responsible.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding, I hope Canadians will understand that the kind of vision we have demonstrated so far, and this Government's new orientation, are in the best interests of all the people in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate my colleague's generosity. I do not expect to need the extra time.
In his very flamboyant speech before lunch the Minister of Public Works (Mr. La Salle) went on for some time about a topic which I think most of us feel quite strongly about, that is, the criticism so many of us levelled at the previous Liberal Government for not creating the jobs this country needed at the time. I recall that the Progressive Conservative Opposition was equally outraged over the fact that unemployment levels were so high and things were so difficult. The amount of job creation taking place was abysmally small. However, the implication which flowed from what the Minister said, as well as from what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and others have said, is that more jobs have been created in the last 14 months than, presumably, in the previous 14 months under the Liberal Government. Goodness knows I do not want to be an apologist for the previous Liberal Government, but I want to put this very clearly on the record. In the 14 months which have passed since the election, there were indeed 415,000 new jobs added to the Canadian workforce. However, in the 14 months previous to the last election, under the Liberal Government, there were 416,000 jobs added to the workforce. If you are going to be technical about it, the Liberals were actually creating more jobs. I just wanted to set those facts out so that people do not think that somehow things have changed. We all agree that
January 17, 1986

the Liberals made an abysmal attempt at job creation, but it turns out that the Tories have been even worse.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext: Shame!

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Indeed, shame on both sides for not creating enough jobs during very difficult times.
In my short remarks this afternoon regarding Bill C-84, an Act which introduces a number of changes to Canada's tax system, 1 want to talk about poverty in Canada. It is fair to say that during the 1970s, poverty in Canada was on the decline. On an annual basis, the number of people defined by Statistics Canada as having an income below the poverty level was actually going down year by year. Unfortunately, during the 1980s, this process was reversed and the number of poor is getting larger and larger. In 1984, some 4.3 million people in Canada were living below the poverty line as defined by the Government. In the next four years, the Canada Council on Social Development indicates that, as a result of many of the measures introduced in the last Budget by the Conservative Government, the number living in poverty will actually increase by 630,000. What that means is that the gap between the haves and the have-nots, the rich and the poor, is actually getting wider. More and more people are entering the poverty ranks than ever before, and it is now escalating at a rate which quite frankly is unprecedented since the 1930s.
One would then assume that the Government would take action to reverse this trend. That would be the only reasonable assumption to make. However, we have seen in the last Budget and in the tax measures we are discussing today quite the contrary. The average Canadians citizen will be much worse off as a result of these tax changes and the wealthier will actually be better off. To be more precise, let us consider an average family consisting of a mother, father and two children and assume that one of the spouses earns the income for that family. As a result of the increased taxes in this Budget, that family earning an annual income of $15,000 will actually lose $2,270 over the next five years. In other words, such a family will be much poorer in the next fives years as a result of this Budget.
[DOT] (MIO)
If this family has an income of $35,000, it will also lose the considerable amount of $4,216 over the next five years as a result of increased taxes. However, the situation changes with upper-income earners. Those earning an income of over $80,000 will gain $5,662 in the next five years as a result of tax changes. The rich are getting richer and the middle class and poor of Canada are becoming poorer as a result of the provisions to change the tax system of Canada that we are discussing today.
There are serious problems with some of the provisions we are debating today. For example, there is the change to capital gains legislation. We have always been concerned that those people who derive their income from capital gains are only taxed on half while the other half of their income from capital gains is tax free. The Government is making the situation
Income Tax Act, 1986
worse by allowing those who derive their income or part of their income from capital gains an exemption from capital gains tax on a lifetime accumulation of $500,000.
An individual who earns an income from capital gains will not have to pay income tax this year on $20,000. This increases yearly until it accumulates to $500,000. However, ordinary wage earners pay taxes at source as they always have, with very few deductions, loopholes or tax exemptions at their disposal. The heavier burden is being placed on the backs of working people in this country while those whose income is derived from capital gains will not pay any tax on a major portion of that income. Statistics show that only 4 per cent of Canadians declare capital gains on their income tax. This major provision, which is meant to revolutionize investment in Canada, will only benefit 4 per cent of Canadians.
Another provision for tax changes is the increase in the ceilings for RRSPs. The Government is saying that the amount people may set aside tax free at the end of the year for their retirement will be increased to $15,000 a year. However, what must one's income be to be eligible for this increase in exemption? It must be $86,000 a year. How many Canadians have incomes in excess of $86,000 so they may benefit from this provision? Furthermore, do these Canadians need help to provide for their retirement at a cost to Canadian taxpayers, at the cost of deficit increase, and at the cost of social programs? We cannot emphasize enough that the provisions of this Budget and its tax changes are only assisting a handful of upper income Canadians at the expense of ordinary Canadians.
The same can be said with respect to provisions affecting the corporate tax. The legislation assists the larger corporations rather than small and medium sized business. Even today, thanks to previous Liberal Governments, middle and small businesses actually have a higher effective tax rate than larger corporations. The corporate tax changes we are discussing are biased heavily in favour of large corporations at the expense of the small and medium sized business sector.
I received many petitions in the mail today from the constituency of Kamloops-Shuswap. My constituents have been complaining about the increase in gasoline sales tax. They believed that they would see a decrease in the price of gas at the pumps as a result of the decreasing price of oil on the world markets. However, on January 1 the tax on gasoline went up for everyone in the country. There is no doubt that this discriminates against certain Canadians, particularly those who live in regions of Canada where goods and foodstuffs must be transported long distances, and those Canadians must travel farther as opposed to Canadians in central Canada. It is essentially a tax on distance, which is a bias against western Canadians in such a case.
The Government has decided to increase sales tax at this sensitive time in our recovery. The Minister tells us that the Government will derive some $1.6 billion this year and next year from the increased sales tax and excise tax on gasoline which will proportionately have a more severe impact on lower income families. That $1.6 billion will come from the pockets,
9900

January 17, 1986
Income Tax Act, 1986
purses and wallets of low and middle income Canadians in order to compensate for massive tax breaks given to upper income earners and the larger corporate sector in many cases. This is a redistribution of income from the bottom to the top- a Robin Hood in reverse approach to taxation.
There is a trend in our tax system. The first Government Member who spoke stated that the Government was taking a new and clear direction. It is not so much a new direction, but I agree that it is perhaps an acceleration to a clear direction toward a tax system of consumption. It is a tax on disposable income with no tax or a deferral of tax on savings, interest and investments. We are moving to an era of tax on consumption, which is definitely biased in favour of those who obtain their income through capital gains from the stock markets, investments and savings. The savings and investments of those with large disposable incomes are untouched by the tax man.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
I am just taking this from the book given to me by the Minister of Finance. He says that it will cost $440 million this year. What will we get in return? If the Minister could guarantee that a loss of $440 million to the Treasury of the country will result in massive job creation or even a considerable amount of productivity, I would not be so concerned. However, there is absolutely no evidence that this will happen because there is no accountability in the tax system. It is wrong to add more loopholes year after year without knowing what we are getting in return for that lost revenue.
I know Mr. Speaker, you are asking yourself how much in lost revenue we are talking about, Mr. Speaker. What is our tax system costing the people of Canada? The Auditor General does now know. He looks carefully at the books and says: "This is costing us a great deal of money. All of these tax exemptions, loopholes, are costing us a lot of money, somewhere between $30 billion and $50 billion a year". Think of it, Mr. Speaker. The Auditor General cannot determine what it costs because there is no accountability.
I remember Mr. Lalonde, the Liberal Finance Minister, introduced what was called a scientific research and development tax credit in 1983. He said that it would result in all sorts of research and development. It was going to cost the taxpayers about $100 million to accomplish all of this research and development in new scientific experimentation and the
like. After some analysis was done and a good deal of prodding by Opposition Members, it was found that it was costing us, at that time, at least $1.5 billion and increasing, approaching $2 billion. Only a few months earlier Mr. Lalonde had said it would cost about $100 million.
There was no accountability. Goodness knows if Opposition Members had not been doing their work and created enough pressure to expose this boondoggle, I cannot imagine what would be going on. Individuals were putting together shell companies and collecting from the federal Government $10 million, $15 million and in some cases as much as $42 million in cash and not doing anything with it. It was very fraudulant in some cases, but obviously it was a tax exemption that was a total mistake which had not been thought through carefully at all.
It is for these reasons that we decided as the New Democratic Party to carry out a probe of our tax system. We are calling it Tax Probe 86. A number of members of the NDP caucus will be travelling across the country talking to knowledgeable people in the various areas of the economy, the forest industry, the agricultural industry, the small business sector, women's and various social groups, tax experts, tax lawyers and advisers in an attempt to identify which of the tax expenditures up to perhaps $50 billion-of lost revenue-is giving us something in return.
We need to establish some accountability for our present tax system. Is our tax system fair? I do not think anybody would say it is fair today, but how can we make our system more fair, more accountable, more effective and more efficient? That is the mandate that we are taking upon ourselves as a result of our initiative called Tax Probe 86.
I suppose if there is one thing we must do, it is to take tax reform and place it more on the public policy agenda and perhaps try to place it on the political agenda of the country.
I remember that in 1984 during the federal election campaign the NDP suggested that we should have a minimum tax. Some people in Canada are making incomes of $400,000 and $600,000 plus, and many are not paying income tax, not even a cent. We felt that that was wrong. We felt that it was indicative of an unfair tax system. Ronald Reagan in the United States moved to change that. We felt that Canada should do the same. The Liberals agreed, and even the Prime Minister agreed during the debates in the 1984 election. The Government did introduce a minimum tax, but it is a disaster, Mr. Speaker.
The minimum tax makes the tax system much more complex. Here is a Government that was going to simplify the tax system, yet one of its first changes was to make the tax system much more complicated. There is much more red tape for small business. The Government needs to hire an additional number of people for Revenue Canada to read these doubled up tax forms. The Government is increasing the bureaucracy of Revenue Canada.
Consider what the Government is doing. It is saying that all of those exemptions that upper income earners have used over

the years can be parlayed over the next seven years. It is like exemption or loop-hole averaging. If you cannot use the exemption this year, use it next year or the following year. Financial writers and tax experts writing in the various learned journals are pulling out their hair and saying that this is going to cause an absolute financial adviser's nightmare. What are the implications of rolling over all of these exemptions year after year and parlaying them?
In an effort to introduce a minimum tax, the Government has created more and more fuzz, with more complexity. It is changing the tax system more than ever into an network of impossible passages which the average taxpayer must attempt to manipulate.
Bill C-84 is a reflection of the Government's last Budget introduced a few months ago. It reflects an attempt by the Government to improve the situation of Canada as perceived by the Minister of Finance. He gave a speech to the Canadian Economic Association in Montreal in May, 1985, and said at that time, "No matter how we define the term, Canada has an acute shortage of rich people". The Minister has done his best, using the tax system, to assist more and more people to become richer. One could argue in an academic debate about the merits of doing that, but not at the expense of ordinary Canadians, not at the expense of small business, farmers and fishermen. But that is exactly what Bill C-84 does. It provides tax breaks and, in some cases, almost a financial bonanza for a handful of upper income earners and large corporations. For the average Canadian it imposes additional tax burdens at a time when that is exactly the wrong initiative to be taking. We should be encouraging people to use their disposable incomes to assist and invest in local business, to purchase needed goods and services in local communities helping the small business sector to expand, develop and create jobs. To take disposable income out of the pockets and wallets of ordinary Canadians to pay off the bank bail-outs and to pay for the huge new exemptions being given to a handful of upper income Canadians is wrong. That is the reason we are going to oppose this legislation when we vote.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: Are there any questions and comments? If not, we will resume debate. The Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson).

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Official Opposition has said, since the Budget was brought down that it is an unfair Budget. We have also felt constrained to use the very harsh word sneaky about it. That is not a word one would use lightly. Unfortunately, it is a word that is appropriate for the process with which we are dealing.
When I talk first about the unfairness of the Budget, I refer primarily to the deindexation of the personal income tax system on the one hand, and the capital gains tax exemption on the other.
Deindexing the personal tax system will quietly rob thousands of low and middle income earners whereas the $500,000 capital gains tax exemption is an up-front, no strings gift to a wealthy minority. Personal tax deindexation is targeted and
Income Tax Act, 1986
calculated to strip billions of dollars from low and middle income individuals and families, whereas the capital gains exemption is completely open-ended, not guaranteed to benefit Canada in any way, except to fatten the wallets of the well-to-do.
This measure could have been targeted in ways which would make it more acceptable.lt could have been targeted to owners of family farms or to owners of family businesses. It could have been targeted, as the amendment of the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston) would have done, to Canadian businesses. None of that was done. We have an open-ended system from which people can benefit even if their gains come from art, jewellery, boats, condominiums in Florida or racehorses in Kentucky. There is no requirement that people benefiting from this should invest a dime in any Canadian business or do anything for the Canadian economy.
Whereas the personal tax deindexation will simply extract more tax from those least able to pay, the capital gains exemption will put more money into the pockets and bank accounts of those with the highest incomes. In fact, 64 per cent of the benefits of this program will go to 4 per cent of Canadians, those with the highest incomes. Because the personal tax deindexation, like the sales and excise tax increases, is broadly based with a cumulative effect, its negative effect is not readily apparent. This is why we have felt obliged to use the harsh word "sneaky".
The Minister finally introduced his Budget. As our Leader pointed out earlier today, it was the longest interval in Canadian history between an election and the introduction of a Budget. However, when the Minister finally introduced his Budget following, we were told, extensive consultations, he did not say that he was introducing an across the board tax increase of 3 per cent. What was quietly slid in was the deindexation of the personal tax exemption. Deindexation means that the Government is proposing to do away with the indexation of personal tax exemptions except when the Consumer Price Index exceeds 3 per cent. When the CPI exceeds 3 per cent, the Government will still be taxing that first 3 per cent. As the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount explained, the effect is to transfer the assets of Canadians over to the Government in large amounts. The actions of the Government have belied the rhetoric about fiscal responsibility. It will amass $4.3 billion in 1990-91 through this measure. When we ask why the Government is leaning so heavily on low and middle-income earners for tax revenues, we are told that it is important to reduce the deficit and that fiscal responsibility must be brought to bear. We are all concerned about the deficit, but when we look at the large amounts in our deficits, we find that the two worrisome amounts are the payments to service the national debt and the expenditures on unemployment insurance. Clearly any responsible attempt to reduce the deficit must be primarily based upon job creation, because if people are employed, not only do they not need to draw unemployment insurance, but they are able to pay more tax, they are able to purchase more, and they are able to stimulate

January 17, 1986
Income Tax Act, 1986
the economy and continue the consumer-led recovery we are just starting to see.
However, in the Budget do we see anything that will encourage job creation? No. In the capital gains exemption we see a measure which will cost the Government billions of dollars in foregone revenue with no guarantee whatever of any return. Surely it is inconsistent for the Government to tax low and middle-income earners within an inch of their lives, while at the same time it gives lavish and unsolicited tax breaks to those at the higher income levels. For the Government to hand out a tax give-away of this magnitude without any requirement for benefit to the Canadian economy is not only inconsistent but is foolish.
Millions of Canadians have been told by the Government that it cannot afford to give them protection from inflation and that they must help pay to bring down the deficit. Then the Government offers a $500,000 capital gains exemption, a tax bonanza for the few who are wealthy enough to take advantage of it, and we are told to have faith that this money will find its way into the Canadian economy and will create jobs. However, people with $15,000 incomes will be paying 36 per cent more in taxes over the next four years. When we add in all the measures in the Budget-higher sales taxes, new sales taxes and reduced inflation protection-they will certainly pay, but it is not at all clear where these tax revenues will be applied.
What will the Government do with all the money it is taking out of the pockets of middle-income Canadians? Perhaps this tax revenue will replace the billions of dollars the Government is giving away to the multinational oil companies, amounting to $2.5 billion in 1990-91. We have heard great statements of faith from the Government that investment in the oil patch will create jobs, but it has not explained how.
Perhaps the Government will apply these consumer tax revenues to the almost billion dollar tax exemption it gave to Olympia & York, or maybe the Government will use this taxpayers' money to make up for some of its ill-advised investment as a result of the two bank failures which will cost Canadian taxpayers somewhere in the order of $2 billion.
The point is that in none of these multimillion dollar giveaways did the Government appear to have deficit reduction or fiscal responsibility in mind.
We are not fooled and taxpayers are not fooled by a Government which says that it must have tax on pet food, even if it is for a guide-dog for a blind person, in order to help reduce the deficit, and that it must reduce protection from inflation for the poor and middle-income earners to help reduce the deficit, when it proceeds to give away millions of dollars to large corporations and to the wealthy without any guarantee of benefit to the economy. There is no question that such measures are not only unfair and inconsistent but, 1 would suggest, they are not even sensible. All this money which is being taken out of the domestic economy could be used to help our domestic situation. Low and middle-income earners do not stash away money in savings. They spend their money on the necessities of life; they keep the economy going.
As the Government blindly plans to reduce domestic demand, what is its plan to replace it? Does it think that it can be replaced with exports? What kind of faith is it operating on, and why is it not telling us what is its plan? We suspect that the Government does not have one.
Investment outside Canada is being encouraged by another measure which is not specifically described in Bill C-84 but which remains to be dealt with by regulation under this Bill, that is, the new proposal to allow a larger proportion of investment funds to be invested outside Canada. The plan, as announced in the budget papers, is that for every dollar that a pension fund invests in small business in Canada it will be allowed to invest $3 outside the country. This plan has not been particularly well accepted by pension fund managers. Pension fund managers tend to be cautious in investments, and rightly so.
Because of the very nature of small business, which is entrepreneurial risk taking, there will be problems in finding small business in which to invest that meets the prudent standards of investment by pension funds. Nevertheless, the Government claims that it is helping to provide money for small business. We are told in the budget papers-again it remains to be done by regulation-that pension funds can set up small business investment corporations to this end.
The pension fund managers are not enthusiastic. We had a recommendation before the Finance Committee which objected to the linking of these two objectives. The pension fund managers pointed out that they were in favour of investing in small business when it is prudent, that, in fact, they do this to a large extent, but that they could not see the amounts proposed by the Government as being viable or practical. While they would like some freedom in some cases to invest outside of Canada, they did not want this particular linkage.
Even now there is pension money earmarked for venture capital investment, but it is sitting in short-term securities waiting for the right opportunities, because the right opportunities are not easy to find, that is, right in terms of being a good investment opportunity, but also one that meets the particular requirements for caution and prudence that are involved in dealing with pension funds. The fear among trustees, of course, is always that if they lose money because of a risky investment they could be sued, I think rightly so because people's pension funds, their retirement security, are particularly important to them and not something that can be replaced. If you make a bad investment when you are young, hopefully you can recover it somewhere else, but if a bad investment has taken away your retirement security when you are 70, you are really left in a very vulnerable position. This is why pension fund managers have been-and I hope will continue to be-extremely cautious about investments.
The Government has told us that there could be $10 billion for small busienss as a result of this measure, but what we are hearing from the industry is that at least 95 per cent of all pension fund assets will remain in traditional asset classes.
January 17, 1986

Again we have a measure that the Government put forward apparently without thought, without adequate consultation, and with a lot of smoke and mirrors. It declared it was doing splendid things for small business, but in fact it is not doing so. What it could have done for small business was to have left purchasing power in the hands of low and middle-income Canadians.
This Bill, together with other measures, the sales tax and so on, will result in $11.5 billion being pulled out of the domestic economy. That is a lot of purchasing power which could have done a lot to stimulate demand for small business.
We see before us a Bill that seems to be based on poor economics, one that gives advantages to the wealthy but attacks the lower middle-income earner. It is a Bill that cobbles on a minimum tax in an attempt to show some concern for fairness, but cobbles it on to a complex measure in a way that increases the complexity. It is a sad Bill, it does nothing for Canada, and the only comfort is that since the Minister is, we hear, going to bring in a new Budget soon, perhaps in fact some of these measures here will be cancelled out then.
