I concede that it has been difficult to stick to this commitment, faced with the foolish economic policies of the Government. However, in this case, I want to start my remarks with a sense of fairness which recognizes that the problems are difficult.
The problems which face our country are difficult, as are the problems which face the United States. In fact, the problems which face the entire western world are difficult, in terms of trying to come to grips with a series of extremely large deficits which affect most countries. These are difficult times in terms of a series of interest rate changes which are almost out of the control of the national jurisdiction of our governments. The problems are difficult because there faces us a series of competitive moves by large corporations which, frankly, look to governments for tax breaks and benefits of every possible kind.
All of this is being played off against the backdrop of a liquidity crisis, a crisis which threatens the bankruptcy of not just those Canadian banks which bit the dust in this past year but a whole set of banks which recognize that the large loans they made to Third World and other countries have left them in a very exposed position. It is not an easy time to be a Finance Minister at the start of 1986. In that respect I offer my sympathy to our present Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). However, it is especially difficult to be a Finance Minister at the beginning of 1986 when, in addition to these basic given problems, we are carrying on with a set of ideological blinkers which make it impossible for us to try to tackle the reality of the challenge which faces us.
That is what faces this Government now. Because of the massive set of promises which it made across the country in its irresponsible search for political power, there is a whole host of expenditure commitments to which this Government is now committed. Because of the close relationship with the corporate sector, which has always characterized the Conservative Party, there is a complete tying of hands as far as trying to do something about the revenue side of the picture. Frankly, Mr. Speaker, we get Budgets which are abortions, which do not respond to the realities of the problems which face the country and which do not look for savings in areas where it is legitimate to search and which ignore the possibilities of getting increased revenue from corporate sources in ways which are absolutely basic, straightforward and fair. The consequence of these ideological blinders is that this Government finds itself not fairly putting new burdens on the corporate sector but instead, unfairly giving new give-aways to that corporate sector. It is unfairly giving new gifts and new benefits which do not have as their objective an attempt to increase the efficiency and effectiveness of the operation of the private sector.
We have a Government composed of members who cannot even be good Conservatives because of the bankruptcy of the campaign they ran for power. There is a counter-approach to that which this Government is following. It is a responsible
approach. It is an approach which we as a Party have advocated in this House of Commons. It is an approach which our finance critic has specifically outlined and which we in the action group put forward last April. It is an approach which clearly could take us back to a sense of fiscal responsibility and economic seriousness. It recognizes, first, that a tremendous number of the tax breaks we give are a total waste, not just in terms of their unfairness but in terms of the fact that they give to the rich who do not need the money and who will spend it elsewhere in the world. They are tax breaks which are totally without any economic rationale and which do not face the structural problems which confront this country in 1986. Those are the tax breaks which this Government should eliminate in its next Budget.
I can name some of those tax breaks. A company can borrow money from one of our large banks and can take over another company with absolutely no benefit to the country, to the workers or to the community. It can then write off the interest which it has to pay on the large loan it has taken to pay for this takeover as a tax benefit, which means that the very people who are suffering in many cases from these takeovers are paying out of their tax dollar for the tax break which is allowing them to be victimized. To put it bluntly, the Darcy McKeoughs of this world are paying for their own funeral. I will not shed many tears for Darcy McKeough but I ask what sense it makes in our society to have a tax break like that set in place? What sense does it make to put into effect, as did the past Liberal Government, the scientific research tax credit which has turned into the scientific tax research discredit? It discredits the whole notion of tax benefits for the corporate sector. What possible sense can tax breaks like that make? What possible sense can it make to have a series of benefits set up in the tax system for the large scale corporate sector without a single set of guarantees on the part of the companies which enjoy those tax breaks that they will in fact make a contribution to this country through those tax breaks?
On the other hand, what possible benefit can it be to this country to put a new tax into place on poor and middle income Canadians which will require them to take money out of their pockets which would normally go to small businesses, which in turn would create jobs in their community? Instead, that money goes to make up for these corporate tax breaks. What sort of logic from the point of view of either fairness or some kind of economic sense of effectiveness can be achieved by this sort of tax system? The answer is very clear; none.
We have seen study after study of our tax system which all say in effect that Canada is the greatest mugs game the corporate sector of this world has. It is the greatest poaching ground for fast buck artists from all over the world to come streaming into this country and take advantage of our people. I talked this week with a reporter from the Calgary Herald about the scientific research tax credit. He said that that tax credit has been something which his research shows has been taken advantage of by over 200 American and other foreign entrepreneurs who have come into this country to set up shell companies in order to take advantage of our tax system. It is

quite possible that they will no longer be able to take full advantage of our tax system because at least we managed to grab the horse's tail as it ran out of the empty barn, but even so, there is still the major question as to whether or not we are going to be able to get these people. According to sources of the reporter at the Calgary Herald the Minister of National Revenue has decided to search after these scam companies with just income tax personnel and only under the Income Tax Act. That means that there can be no subpoenas issued outside of this country. There can be no use of the RCMP to do an investigation outside of this country. These fast buck artists who have come in and exploited our country's tax system can quite possibly get off scot-free. There is no logic to that whatsoever. Not to me, not to anyone in this House of whatever Party, not to anyone in the country regardless of the Party they support.
We have to somehow get things right. We have to turn it around. We have to put the tax burden where it belongs, on people and companies who have the capacity to pay. Those of us who have the capacity to pay are not going to be upset about that. My good supporter in the Windsor area, William Tupperman, who owns a great set of furniture stores throughout that part of southwestern Ontario, has no compunction about paying a fair share of taxes. The professionals who vote for us in Amherstburg have no problem with paying fair taxes. What outrages them, what makes them fiercely angry, is to see people earning exactly the same amount of money as they are and taking advantage of loophole after loophole after loophole while escaping their fair share of taxes. This Budget, with its $500,000 capital gains scam, makes it even worse. That is a scam without any control or regulation. It is not even like a MURB. Despite the fact that a MURB might be unfair and open only to certain professional groups, it at least had to be for something here in this country which would create a physical asset in which people could live. However, in the case of this exemption it is quite possible for capital gains to be created on yachts in Florida, jewellery purchased in Mexico, skins collected from Africa and commodity dealings in Chicago, all of which have absolutely no connection with the real economy of this country. These kinds of capital gains are totally useless to the Canadian people and our economy. Yet we have here, prancing happily and smiling gaily, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) saying that this is something which will help Canada. It is going to help the rich and, by doing so, delegitimatize even further our tax system.
I suspect that each of us in this House knows of small business people desperately in need of help. These people will create dozens of jobs if they get that help. They are the ones who should be getting help from this Government, not just because of fairness but because if we continue these tax boondoggles and scams it will be simply unbelievable when Members of the Conservative Party stand up and talk about deficit reduction. The Canadian people will see deficit reduction as simply a way to hide the fact that they are hurting the poor and helping the rich.

Several months have gone by since the 1985 Budget, and being the critic for the Liberal Party in matters relating to small-and medium-sized businesses, I found it essential to prepare a detailed analysis of the impact on Canadian economic growth of the major proposals put forward by the Conservative Government.
The Government has focused its economic strategies on the creation of so-called favourable climates, rather than initiatives directly impacting this country's economic life. The Government discharges its responsibilities by suggesting that the capital gains tax exemption and the releasing for investment of the money held in RRSPs and other pension funds would have a positive, moving effect on the whole Canadian economy.
Mr. Speaker, since May last two banks have failed. There has been the insurance crisis, and we should be looking at the last statistical report to see how this Government is collecting our taxes. We have seen an increase of nearly half a billion dollars and it was not individuals but mainly companies that had the opportunity to re-establish their income tax payments.
It is imperative in my view that we make a thorough analysis of those measures because they are the cornerstone of the 1985 Budget and they shed a good light on the future economic trends of this Government.
The Budget provides that individuals will be entitled to a lifetime capital gains tax exemption of $500,000. Already, 50 per cent of capital gains were not taxable. This measure, therefore, is introducing a $250,000 tax exemptions.
The Minister of Finance figures that the $500,000 tax exemption on capital gains will result for the federal treasury

invest in small businesses, inview of the fact that the RRSPs and the Registered Retirement Savings Funds account together for a capital pool of some $40 billion. In this document, the PC Government claims that since a total of $160 billion is now accumulated in pension funds, up to $11 billion could be invested in small businesses. An objective analysis of these two investment vehicles will show that the figures put forward by the PC Government are clearly unrealistic and even fallacious.
The Budget would like to encourage RRSP contributors to invest up to 50 per cent of their funds in shares of private Canadian corporations. RRSP contributors, however, must have no connection with the firms in which they would like to invest or with their owners. They can invest directly in small businesses, but not in small businesses belonging to themselves, their relatives or business relations. The provisions concerning arm-length investments are extremely rigid and restricting.
Mr. Speaker, how can anyone suggest that a Canadian investor will be willing to invest in a small business which relies only on the owner himself? There are no board members. The investor cannot rely on five-year financial statements, but only on the ability of one person.
That is the reality; that is what a small business represents.
Mr. Speaker, instead of helping such people by saying "Go and get some capital, use your own pension fund and take 50 per cent to invest", the Government says; "No, you cannot touch it." The Government is willing to trust investors and to say: "There is no limit as far as capital gains are concerned; you can even sell a property in Florida or Italy without paying any capital gains tax." However, when it comes to small businesses, it is not the same story. The Government has to put a stop to it because everyone could take advantage of this provision. Such is the climate of confidence which this Conservative Government is trying to create.
The studies on the creation of businesses in Canada and the United States clearly show that the major sources of financing for small businesses are the businessman himself, his family, his friends and his business relations. Indeed, that is quite normal and understandable. Access to small businesses is always very limited for the investor. Very often, the investor can only rely on his own evaluation of the integrity of the businessman based on his background and on the business contacts the investor has already had with him.
By systematically eliminating the possibility for the businessman himself, his family and business relations to invest in a company, the Government is flying in the face of a basic concept in the development of small businesses.

Mr. Speaker, thank you for giving me an opportunity to speak to what I see as the most important matter facing this country today, and I refer to the rebuilding of our economy, a process we started as soon as we came to power in September 1984. All economic indicators show that what we have done up to now has been positive, and thanks to the removal of bandaid policies, all Canadians can already look to a better and, especially, far more satisfying future for our young people.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-84, an Act to Amend the Income Tax Act, which is part of a series of Bills to enact the tax measures and other proposals announced in the May Budget, this Bill is one of the key instruments of the concept of rebuilding an economy devastated as a result of the irresponsibility of the previous Government. This Bill contains measures inspired by the principles of social justice and equity for all.
Mr. Speaker, this Bill contains draconian measures that will affect people with high incomes and our large financial institutions. It contains measures that the New-Liberal-Democratic Government of the past was always afraid to take, since despite their socialistic vocabulary, they served the interests of the far Right.
Mr. Speaker, this Bill shows, whatever the Official Opposition's irresponsible rhetoric may conclude, that our Government is acting in the interests of the needy and the middle class in this country. It is acting in an almost revolutionary spirit, as revolutionary as the actions, if not the words, of the previous government were reactionary and synonymous with stagnation.
Mr. Speaker, at this point, for the benefit of Canadians, I want to recapitulate what Bill C-84 has to offer this country.
First of all, the capital gains tax exemption. The Budget is proposing an important measure aimed at promoting risktaking and investment in small and large businesses, and to help farmers-my colleague mentioned this point earlier-by offering a cumulative capital gains exemption of up to $500,000 during the lifetime of the taxpayer. This change will be an incentive to Canadians to set up new businesses and help small businesses expand.
The second element of this Bill which has hardly been mentioned in the debate until now is the labour-sponsored venture capital fund whose model was first established in Quebec with the co-operation of the union led by Mr. Laberge. Incidentally, the Thibault plant in my riding was able to use a $750,000 investment from that fund-three-quarters of a million dollars-to create 70 jobs and expand its operations, it now has 190 workers on the payroll. Most of those funds came from company workers. A new tax credit has been proposed to encourage long-term investment by individuals in laboursponsored venture capital organizations set up within a province to maintain or create jobs and stimulate the economy.
The proposed federal tax credit applies to shares purchased by individuals after May 23, 1985. It will be equal to either 20 per cent of the cost of the shares, or the amount required to bring the combined federal and provincial credits to 40 per cent of the shares, whichever is less. That is a new initiative which will enable workers to earn a share of company profits.
Then there are investments, pensions plans and other retirement income plans in small businesses.
The Bill proposes a number of other measures to help small-and medium-sized businesses obtain investment capital through pension funds. First of all, RRSPs and other similar plans will be allowed to buy shares of Canadian-controlled private corporations that are at arm's length from the plan beneficiary.
Second, registered pension plans will be allowed to set up special corporations for tax-exempted investments in small businesses in order to encourage the purchase of shares of small businesses.
Third, pension funds and other deferred income plans will have more flexibility to invest in these limited partnership corporations specializing in small business investments due to the fact that these investments will no longer be consolidated with foreign assets in the computation of the total portfolio-limiting ceiling.
Fourth, pension plans will be authorized to invest three dollars in foreign businesses for every dollar they invest in small Canadian businesses. This way, they will be able to diversify their portfolios easily and create a great many jobs.
The Bill refers also to housing funds. The Budgets proposes to exempt from tax a number of benefits, including low-cost or no-interest loans which employees may obtain from their employers when they must relocate to keep their jobs or take up new positions. This measure will favour workers' mobility and will reflect the fact that housing loans represent for employers a good way to compensate their staff who must move to an area where the cost of living is higher.
This reform Budget deals also with research and development. The tax credits obtained by a small business on the first $2 million spent in research and development current expense will be reimbursed fully, instead of just 40 per cent as is the case now. Other changes will help eliminate the restrictions applicable to the research and development activities which open entitlement to fiscal incentives.
The Budget proposes to make fully refundable the credit accrued to small Canadian-controlled private corporations in respect of current research and development expenditures. The refundable part of the credit unused by these companies is now limited to 40 per cent, as I said earlier. Under the present

provisions, the balance of the unused tax credit may be carried over a maximum of seven years. The new proposal will enable a taxpayer to use all of the earned credit, either to reduce his income tax or to get a refund. That provision will have no expiry date and will apply to eligible expenses incurred after May 23, 1985, as for the other provisions.
Let me now refer to the small business bond, another initiative proposed in this legislation. The bond program will enable farmers and small businesses facing financial difficulty to secure loans at reduced interest rates. The Budget proposed to extend the program for another two years, and to extend it to that type of bonds that will be issued before the end of 1987. The initial expiry date was to be the end of 1985. Another budget proposal would allow farmers and small businesses still tied up with loans obtained under the SMB and the previous small business development bond program, which was in force in 1980 and in 1981, to refinance their loans when falling due if they are facing financial difficulties at the time of refinancing.
Let me also refer to the investment tax credit. That special tax credit, amounting to 50 per cent of manufacturing investments in designated areas, which was introduced in 1980 for a five-year period, was due to expire at the end of 1985. The Budget proposed to extend that special credit until December 1986. It was further proposed that expenses in respect of projects that are not completed by the end of 1986 also provide entitlement to that tax credit. Buildings under construction at the end of 1986 and machinery and equipment ordered in writing before 1986 also will provide entitlement to the credit.
Let me now refer to family support. There has been much talk about it, often in a negative way. But the positive sides are much greater. The child benefit system-that is the family allowances, the child tax credit and the dependent child deductions-is undergoing various changes to provide greater help to lower income families, while reducing benefits now received by higher income families.
The child tax credit, of which my colleague for Champlain (Mr. Champagne) spoke so eloquently yesterday, will increase by $70 in the 1986 taxation year and by $35 in 1987 and 1988. The level of income over which the child tax credit will begin to decrease will be brought down from $26,330 to $23,500.
There is also a point about which little has been said, namely the help provided for the handicapped. In 1985, a $2,590 deduction from taxable income is provided for the handicapped, who are now defined as people suffering from blindness at some time during the year or people who must stay in bed or in a wheel-chair for a considerable part of the day.
Approximately 185,000 people should benefit from this extended definition compared with the 65,000 who now claim such a deduction.
Income Tax Act, 1986
Let us talk about the investment tax credit. Bill C-84 reduces the credit when the taxpayer receives a refund or investment assistance from the public sector or other taxpayers, restricts the possibility of using investment tax credits when there is a change of control, and redefines the classes of share issues which can be used to transfer to outside share investor the unused investment tax credits.
Let us talk about the approach to income generally. The rules governing the distribution of income among members of a same family will be made more stringent to prevent tax avoidance through low interest loans.
Mr. Speaker, I am enthusiastic about all these proposals contained in Bill C-84 and I must say that, in my opinion, our Government is acting as a responsible Government, as a Government which has the interests of Canadians at heart, as a Government which keeps its election promises and which will see to it that our Canadian economy is renewed and continues to develop as all known economic indicators show is now happening.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT RESPECTING LEGAL COUNSEL FOR UNBORN CHILD

speakeroldname: Mr. Lawrence I. O'Neil (Cape Breton Highlands-Canso) moved
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT RESPECTING LEGAL COUNSEL FOR UNBORN CHILD
speechtext:
that Bill C-254, an Act to amend the Criminal Code (legal counsel for unborn child) be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to speak to Bill C-254, an Act to amend the Criminal Code to provide legal counsel for unborn children. It is regrettable that we must debate this Bill and that existing provisions of the Criminal Code are being abused and ignored. At present Section 251 of the Criminal Code purports to protect the unborn children in this country. It purports to balance competing rights. Just what does Section 251 of the Criminal Code require? Section 251 of the Criminal Code requires that before the life of an unborn child can be terminated legally in this coumtry, people appointed by the Board of the medical institution must evaluate an application put forward by a Canadian who wishes to terminate the pregnancy or the life of the unborn Canadian.
The process requires that these medical people decide whether the health or life of the mother is jeopardized by continuing the pregnancy. That is what Section 251 of the Criminal Code requires of the medical profession in this country. Section 251 requires this because in this country it is not legal to terminate the lives of unborn children on one's sole desire without any grounds whatsoever. The Code requires the doctors to make a decision based on medical evidence.
It sounds very good, but in practice we have a situation in hospitals from the east coast to the west coast where doctors gather routinely for perhaps one half hour or an hour each week and over this period of time, these medical people decide whether the lives of 60 or perhaps 100 unborn Canadians should be terminated.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT RESPECTING LEGAL COUNSEL FOR UNBORN CHILD
speechtext: Shame!

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT RESPECTING LEGAL COUNSEL FOR UNBORN CHILD
speechtext:
The unborn child will be very fortunate if his case or her case is given more than 60 seconds of consideration by the people in this country who have the responsibility to decide whether that life shall end or shall continue. That is the practice, and in my view that is illegal. The practice is outside the spirit and the legal requirements of the Criminal Code. We have a situation in this country where many people have decided to turn a blind eye to the strict requirements of the Criminal Code and to allow this flagrant abuse of the rights of unborn children to continue. The question is what can be done about this abuse? Many would say that we should repeal Section 251 altogether, and perhaps that is not a bad idea in some cases. Another idea is to make an amendment to the Criminal Code which is consistent with the spirit and the design of that Section which was designed to provide a judicial
or quasi-judicial environment in which the rights of the unborn child would be protected. It is obvious that at the present time when these hearings occur that there is no spokesperson for the unborn Canadian, that the process has become one of rubber-stamping.
It is for this reason that I have introduced Bill C-254, an Act to amend the Criminal Code, that would require the presence of legal counsel for unborn children, legal counsel who would work to ensure that the rights and representations of the unborn Canadian are made. When I advance this concept I am not advancing something which is revolutionary. Section 251, as I said earlier, is a recognition of the rights of unborn Canadians. Abortion is illegal in this country, in general terms, and legal only in certain exceptional cases, because we as a society have recognized the rights of unborn children to continue.
This is consistent with the rights of unborn Canadians as protected by the Canadian Bill of Rights, which in Part 1(a) states that "(a) the right of the individual to life, liberty, security of the person and enjoyment of property, and the right not to be deprived thereof except by due process of law;" must be protected in Canada.
That is a guiding principle of our society, and a guiding principle of our judiciary system. In this case is being flagrantly abused. Similarly, Section 197 of the Criminal Code is very interesting because it imposes a legal duty on everyone as a parent, foster parent, guardian or head of a family to provide the necessities of life for a child under the age of 16 years. An unborn child is a child, by definition, and it is under 16 years of age. There are very similar sections in the Criminal Code in which we recognize the rights of unborn Canadians.
There are protections in an area of law known as tort law whereby an unborn child can sue, for example, after birth for injuries and wrongs that were inflicted upon it prior to its birth. These protections are well recognized in our body of law. Therefore, when I advocate that the unborn child has in fact certain rights that must be protected, I am simply outlining what is part of our body of common and codified law today.
The unborn child has certain rights and protection with respect to the inheritance of property. Those are well recognized and outlined in various court judgments. 1 found it quite interesting two years ago to read in The Globe and Mail a front page story in which a Family Court Judge acting under child welfare legislation held that a foetus deserved the shield of the law. That was a decision by a Family Court Judge in Kenora. He ruled that a foetus, or an unborn child, was abused because its mother refused to stop her excessive drinking during the pregnancy and the unborn child was in need of protection under child welfare law.
It is well recognized that an unborn child is something special in our society and has life. We live in an era when the knowledge of unborn life, the biological reality is becoming even more known to all Canadians. It is being taught at elementary and high school levels and the biological details of life are well known and widely accepted. I have here an issue of Newsweek magazine of January 11, 1982. The cover story is
January 17, 1986

"How Life Begins Biology's New Frontier". In this article, which is in a popular magazine, the author's outline states biological information which is revolutionary in our day. For example it portrays that at three weeks the heart of an unborn child beats and the brain begins to develop. At four weeks limb buds appear. At five weeks the brain has divided into three parts and limbs to grow. This is just some indication of the biological reality. It is for that reason that we are in a better position than any of our predecessors to express an informed view on this question of life. There are those who say that this is not life and that we must treat the unborn child as if he or she were nothing more than a fingernail.
As I sat in the Chamber yesterday, I found it quite interesting to hear from other Members their views on the value of children on our society and on the value of family life. I will repeat for Hon. Members who are here today and for the record some quite interesting comments that were made yesterday. I am reading from page 9855 of Hansard:
They have refused to listen despite the sense that any civilized society has that children are a common concern, a common responsibility and a responsibility which all of us in society have to defend.
That, Mr. Speaker, is a position which I wholeheartedly endorse. It goes on:
Any society deserves to give such children full respect-
Mr. Speaker, this debate deals with justice... We want a society where the children are the pride of their country.
1 agree. Those comments were made by the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon), a member of the New Democratic Party, just yesterday in this Chamber. As well, I would like to turn to some comments made by the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone), a member of the Liberal Party. She had this to say on the debate that took place yesterday in the Chamber, as reported at page 9859 of Hansard-.
The family allowance confirms the value of child rearing to society at large. It is the sole, consistent economic recognition of the contribution of all mothers in our society.
I agree with that, but the recognition of the value of the child must begin with the life of the child. It is widely accepted today that life begins well before birth and that what happens at birth is that the child emerges into a new context. It is well recognized that the rights of unborn Canadians do exist quite apart from the abortion issue.
I know some of my colleagues would like to register their support for this initiative. In conclusion, I would like to say that what I have presented to the House today is an opportunity to ensure that the widespread practices in hospitals across the country, the widespread violations of the Criminal Code, come to an end. I am asking the House to bring the law in line with the biological reality as we know it.
I have reviewed for the House the protections granted by Section 251 of the Criminal Code, the so-called abortion Section. That Section of the Criminal Code sets up a regime designed to protect the rights of unborn children. Our law
Criminal Code
makers and enforcers have allowed society to turn a blind eye to the abuse that is taking place. These offences that are occurring across the country in our hospitals are criminal offences and it is time that we moved to ensure that the practices in this country reflects the law in this country.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT RESPECTING LEGAL COUNSEL FOR UNBORN CHILD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first 1 would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Cape Breton High-lands-Canso (Mr. O'Neil) for sponsoring a very good piece of legislation. Bill C-254 was, I am sure, inspired by a sense of indignation at the widespread increase in the abortion rate. Our discussion today will provide another chapter to the long history of the abortion debate in this House.
This Bill represents a great opportunity for agreement within the House. It will have the effect of guaranteeing the presence of legal representation for the unborn child at the therapeutic abortion committee that would pass judgment on the mother's intention to have an abortion. This is not a new idea. Under our legal system, people accused of crimes have always enjoyed a fundamental right to the advice and counsel of a lawyer to support their defence when standing for trial. This is one of the basic elements of the principles of fundamental justice that are enshrined in our Constitution.
Although the right to counsel is a fundamental right, its application is somewhat inconsistent. In Canada, this right has never been withheld from an accused person. However, thousands of unborn children who are not accused but innocent are tried, sentenced and executed every day without the right to counsel.
In my mind, there is no greater contradiction within our system of justice than that, while civil libertarians are doing everything to extend the rights of criminals, the rights of totally innocent Canadians are so neglected. I still cannot understand why some people uphold the death penalty for innocent, unborn children while proclaiming that they stand for the sanctity of life.
Extending the right to counsel to unborn children is the type of proposal the House should support unanimously. In doing so, we would not be guilty of so many of the so-called offences that prevent action on the question of abortion. We would not be legislating morality. The effect of this Bill would be to improve the quality of whatever decision is made by a mother, her doctor and the therapeutic abortion committee.
Decisions are made by weighing information and choosing between alternatives. This Bill would allow the unborn child's legal counsel to present to the committee information about the child's interests. What is to be gained by excluding certain information pertaining to a child's best interests from a decision relating to the pregnancy? The only reason that could exist for not wanting that information presented is the fear that it might influence the mother, perhaps even traumatically, so that she would change her mind. However, is that not the best possible reason for gathering information before a decision is made? This information is so important precisely because it might make a woman think twice about an abortion and it might save the life of her child.

January 17, 1986
Criminal Code
Even radical pro-choice people should be happy when a woman decides not to have an abortion but to keep her baby. They often seem to think that every decision to have an abortion was the best possible choice. I would be delighted to hear someone who is pro-choice say just once that in one case the person had heard about, the decision to have an abortion was a mistake. 1 think this would be a breakthrough.
It would be my hope that the legal counsel acting on behalf of the unborn child present at the therapeutic abortion committee could at least make the case that the unborn child has a right to life. He would be able to describe, depending upon the stage of pregnancy, the development of hands, feet, a face, hair or fingernails. He might describe the movements of the child, its weight and the fact that its heart had already started to beat. He might bring up the point about the thousands of Canadian families that would welcome the baby with love into their own homes, bearing in mind that in Ontario, there is a five-year waiting periof for those who wish to adopt. He might suggest to the mother the joy she would receive from keeping the baby herself.
Finally, legal counsel for the baby might indicate what would happen to the child if the decision to have an abortion were followed through with. He might describe how the baby's body is cut to pieces by a sharp scraper when the D and C technique is used or how it is pulled apart by a powerful suction tube during a suction abortion. As well, there is the hypernatremic abortion in which the baby is poisoned, its skin is burned by a powerful salt solution and some days later, after suffering, expelled. The legal counsel might inform the mother for the first time that the child was facing a painful and lingering death. I think a mother would want to know that and should know that. I also think that there is a good chance that it would change her mind about having an abortion.
A woman does not always have access to all of this information and particularly to the good things about childbirth and the bad things about abortion. The idea of extending civil and human rights to unborn children is not a new one. In fact, apart from the right to life and to the due process of law, unborn children, in many legal respects, are fully recognized as persons.
The question of when life begins, I believe, is at conception. Medical science can identify when each process that is essential to life, such as the functioning of the heart and other organs, begins. However, there is a necessity to incorporate some definition of life into a society's system of laws. In order to charge someone with murder one has to spell out exactly what the life is that one is accused of ending. If everyone agreed that life began at conception, then people such as Dr. Henry Morgentaler could be found guilty of murder.
In our system of laws there are many indications that our society fully recognizes unborn children as legal persons, fully entitled to the protection we all enjoy under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Common law relating to property generally recognizes the unborn child as a person. A child can be
the benefactor of an estate left to him or her in a will. Counsel acting on behalf of an unborn child can petition the courts for inclusion of the unborn child in a will that leaves an estate to other children in the family. This even holds if those other children are identified explicitly by name and the unborn child is not mentioned.
There is an implicit common law contract recognized in the right of an infant to the necessities of life. Similar protection is extended to an unborn child, if the mother has an intention to continue with her pregnancy.
Our legal system also provides in other ways for unborn children. They are given the status of persons and can be eligible for benefits under workers' compensation and accident benefits legislation. This indicates to me that not only does society recognize the fact that unborn children have their own interests, but that we also have an interest in the welfare of unborn children.
Unborn children also have rights to receive compensation for criminal injuries. If a pregnant women is injured through violence or negligence on the part of someone else, and the unborn child suffers as well, then they have an equally well grounded legal entitlement. The contradiction of this arrangement is the fact that if a child dies before it is born, then its rights as a person cannot be represented or defended.
Unborn children, then, are protected by most rights except for the right to life itself, which is the most fundamentally important one as far as our society is concerned. Even the Criminal Code sections related to abortion seem to recognize that the unborn child is valued by society. Under our laws abortion is an indictable criminal offence for both the mother and the doctor, if they do not follow the required procedure with a therapeutic abortion committee. Unfortunately, the law also provides two massive loopholes. One is the role of therapeutic abortion committees, which provide nothing more than a rubber-stamping process, in a great many instances. The other loophole is being tragically exploited in Ontario. Dr. Morgentaler is allowed to continued the operation of his abortion clinic in outright defiance of the law because it is not being enforced. This is something upon which 1 strongly urge the Government of Ontario to take proper action.
However, it is important to note that one can receive an abortion by going around the law. The law itself still forbids abortions in most cases. This is because the law recognizes that unborn children are entitled to protection of the law to the same extent as the rest of Canadians. It is for exactly this reason that I ask the House today to take the step which would guarantee the right to counsel for unborn children. It is not a big step, but it is a step in the right direction. If we do not take this step it is because we have fallen into a trap which has been seen again and again throughout history. 1 am speaking of the exploitation of the weak by the powerful. The extent to which we are civilized and human is the measure by which the weak enjoy the protection of our society.
One opponent of abortion described the problem like this:
Slavery, witch-hunts, and wars have all been justified by their perpetrators on the ground that they thought their victims to be less than fully human.
January 17, 1986

Abortion has claimed more lives than slavery, witch-hunts, and wars put together. In Canada, over the last 15 years, there have been close to one million deaths due to abortion. If one were to add up the deaths caused by drowning, car accidents, and warfare over the last 50 years, one would see that the figure comes to about one-third of that for abortions.
I find it ironic that in a day and age when we spend billions of dollars on medical research to save lives at the same time we allow the killing of healthy baby boys and girls. We have hospitals which on one floor are exercising all the medical research and expertise possible to save lives while on another floor of the same hospital hundreds and thousands of unborn children are being killed. It is time our society lived up to its responsibility and that we as legislators acted in the name of justice and human dignity instead of expedience, opportunism and convenience.
The Bill before us today is an example of the type of Bill which I think all Members of the House can and should support. It is unique in the respect that it represents some substantial progress regarding the tragedy our country faces over the abortion issue. I hope that we will all consider giving this Bill our full support today.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT RESPECTING LEGAL COUNSEL FOR UNBORN CHILD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know that I can say that I am pleased to be standing today in my place to take part in this debate since it seems to me that every two or three weeks we seem to be debating the same issue. It is a very important question. However, it is a question on which I believe it would be hard for this House to reach a consensus. As well, I believe there is really no full consensus on the issue in Canada today.
In preparation for the debate today I looked not only at the Bill but at the explanatory note. I read Section 251 of the Criminal Code as it stands at the present time. I wish to read part of that section into the record for those who may not be aware of it. Section 251(1) states:
Every one who, with intent to procure the miscarriage of a female person, whether or not she is pregnant, uses any means for the purpose of carrying out his intention is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for life.
Section 251(2) states:
Every female person who, being pregnant, with intent to procure her own miscarriage, uses any means or permits any means to be used for the purpose of carrying out her intentions is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for two years.
The section goes on to qualify what some of the terms mean and it then states certain exceptions, such as the case of a therapeutic abortion committee at an accredited or approved hospital.
It seems to me that one whole section has been left out. I say this with not a great deal of seriousness. However, it does point out something which I am sure male Members of the House might like to consider. If the Bill is referred to a committee I wonder if the Member who proposed the Bill would consider another amendment to the Criminal Code which would state the following:
Criminal Code
Every person who impregnates a woman with male sperm causing her to be pregnant against her will is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for life.
It seems to me that makes just as much sense as some of the things we already have in the Criminal Code. Perhaps this kind of amendment would cause people to consider, first, who causes unwanted pregnancies. That brings us to the question before us today; who causes the unwanted pregnancies? It is pretty evident that without the male sperm there would be no pregnancy, therefore, the man in each case has a very major responsibility. Second, who makes the very difficult and painful decision as what should or should not be done about an unwanted pregnancy? I think the answer is perfectly clear, certainly to the women in this House. It is the woman who is going to have to deal with this very painful decision and no one can tell me that any woman faced with an unwanted pregnancy will not face a very, very painful decision, particularly if she decides that she has no alternative but to consider abortion.
Finally, who is faced with the responsibility of rearing a child if the pregnancy is continued and who often is left alone without resources to rear that child? There again, we know that it is the woman who is responsible for this and we have a lot of statistics to show that most of those women do not have adequate finances. I believe some of the witnesses to the divorce Bill hearings would substantiate the fact that these women do not have adequate support and certainly increasing numbers of women are left alone with the responsibility of their children with no support whatsoever. I would say, particularly to the male Members of this House, that it is indeed a very serious and difficult emotional question which faces women who have been made pregnant and who are forced to consider what they should do in the case of an unwanted pregnancy.
We in this House have very different points of view-and it is easy to get very uptight about this. I do myself-so it is very important that we look at the various areas on which perhaps we can agree. The whole question of abortion is fraught with emotion on all sides. We know this. I would hope we can learn somehow to respect our different points of view and perhaps not discuss it when we know there is absolutely no potential for reasonable communication. I also hope that we can agree that no woman really wants an abortion and those women who are driven to seek one usually do so because they have little or no alternative. I do not think any feminist group advocates abortion as a method of birth control. That argument is passe. I do not know of any feminists, including myself, who feel that abortion is a positive thing. It is not. No one really favours abortion. However, women, particularly young women, poor women and women under a lot of stress, really have no other alternative when they are left in a pregnant state. They are unable to care for their child and they have no other alternative. It is a desperate situation in which a woman finds herself and so very often they are alone. I do not feel we give enough consideration to this point.

January 17, 1986
Criminal Code
I also hope that we in this House can agree that it would be far better to put our efforts into prevention. Surely we can work together on that even though we might have different philosophies about the whole question of choice of abortion. 1 would hope we could somehow work together to develop programs and to work with the Ministers responsible so that we could have far more research into adequate methods of contraception. I feel we should have much greater research into contraception as it applies to men. I feel this whole area has been neglected. We know there are many, many cases where the pill and other methods of contraception have had very negative side effects. We must find more effective methods of contraception. I hope that all of us in this House agree that it is far better, far more humane and far more important to prevent unwanted pregnancies than for a woman to be faced with the situation of having to consider an abortion.
Men have a great responsibility in this area and they are not assuming their responsibility. I would say that many of the supporters of this Bill which is before the House are probably not doing their part to ensure that we are putting all of our efforts into prevention. I hope that we can agree to put much more research into contraceptive methods as well as, of course, education, particularly for young people. Many parents need help because they are not comfortable discussing matters of sexuality, family planning and birth control methods. I hope as well that we can agree that despite our very different and strong emotional and personal views on the question of abortion that we, as Members of Parliament do not have the right to use our position as elected Members of Parliament to introduce laws which would arbitrarily impose our views on others. We must be very careful in the way we exercise the power we have. It is not up to me to force a woman to have an abortion or to say she cannot have an abortion when she is pregnant. It is not up to me to say. It is not up to me to bring in laws which are going to force a woman to go to a back street abortionist because we are restricting access to a safe medical procedure. It is up to the woman. It is an individual matter. It is not up to us to tell that woman and her doctor what should be done in an individual case.
Professor Charles Kelbey, a law professor, I believe, said in an article in Newsweek that when highly emotionally charged issues have to be resolved in law, it is far better to come down on the side of freedom than on the side of prohibition. Therefore, I would say to my colleagues that I respect their vies. I know many of their views are different from mine and mine are different from theirs and I believe we must respect each other's views. We surely have no right to impose our views on another person. I think the whole question of choice is important. It is not pro-abortion to be in favour of choice. None of us, I hope, are pro-abortion. We in this Party cannot support this Bill. It would appear that the intent is to further complicate procedures and make it more difficult for women to have access to safe medical abortions. Access to abortions is already far too restricted. I am not going to get into the whole question of when life begins because I believe that is something which will always be a personal and philosophical view and we could
argue forever and not agree on that. 1 agree with my friend that the present law is not being carried out because access to abortion is far too restricted. There are very few hospitals in maritime, northern or rural communities, for example, where women have any choice at all. The present law requires, as we know, that a woman present her case before a therapeutic abortion committee of at least three doctors in an accredited or approved hospital. I know in my province of British Columbia, there are a number of hospitals which no longer have therapeutic committees. This is making it more difficult for women. My doctor tells me that many women from Victoria, for example, have no access and are going to the U.S. as a result. That is the only choice they have.
I have no facts to substantiate this but I would hazard a guess that the fact there is no access to abortions is not stopping unwanted pregnancies. What are women doing? 1 am sure they are taking illegal steps to have abortions. Is that what Members want? Do they want women to die? That seems to me to be the final outcome of this kind of restrictive philosophy which does not leave the matter to individual choice.
Approximately 75 per cent of our hospitals do not have therapeutic abortion committees and therefore do not offer the service to their surrounding areas. I received letters last year from the Canadian Medical Association which feels there should be some reconsideration of the concept of a committee because it gets very complex. They feel it should be really more of a medical decision. However, there should be therapeutic abortion committees in accredited hospitals and they should be available in all regions of Canada. It does not make sense to have this provision in our law and then not have the service available in certain communities.
With all due respect to my friend who brings this Bill forward, I wonder if he is aware of some of the following facts. First, making abortions more difficult to obtain will not cut back on the number of women who are seeking and obtaining abortions. It will not stop them. The only thing that will stop unwanted pregnancies and abortions is prevention. Let's get together and start working on more prevention.
Another fact is that if there is no access to abortions, these women will simply go back to obtaining unsafe abortions where they may die or be maimed for life. That is what the situation used to be like. If they are wealthy, of course, the wives and perhaps the daughters or partners of Members of Parliament and people with that kind of a salary, what are they going to do? They are probably going to go across the line to states which have easy access to abortions, or they are going to go to private medical care of some kind. What if you are a poor woman or adolescent girl? There are girls 14, 15 and 16 pregnant now and if we carry through with this philosophy we will be forcing them to go ahead and have babies. This will be destructive to both the child and the young mothers.
I deplore the fact that this is happening just as much as other Members. However, the fact is that in countries where
January 17, 1986

abortions are illegal, women continue to need and get abortions. There have been unwanted pregnancies throughout history. We have heard stories of women who used a hot bath and a bottle of gin to get rid of an unwanted pregnancy. It is going to happen no matter what policy we have concerning access to abortion. What we need is prevention. I ask Members, regardless of their views on our present Criminal Code, to give much more emphasis to prevention. That is what we need.
What of women who live far from centres where these services are available? If they cannot afford to travel or to have other children in the family looked after while they are gone, or whatever the reason is, they simply become prime targets for back room butchers or unsafe abortion methods. There are long delays which are difficult for both the woman and her doctor because they do not have adequate access and as a result the pregnancy often goes on too long.
I have many, many other points I would like to make and I am sure that since this matter keeps coming up again and again I will have further opportunities to make them. However, I implore my fellow Members to think about this. It is very tempting, because of our gut emotions, to polarize this situation. I feel as strongly as anyone about this issue, but I wish we could work together on the positive things that we can agree on. Let us really work together to try and make sure that there is adequate family planning, information and services available. Instead of cutting back on planned parenthood we should be supporting the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) in obtaining more money for more adequate research and programs which are targeted to young adolescents to help them deal with their sexuality and avoid situations which will ruin their lives. We should have family planning in every community. I would certainly hope that we could all work together on all methods of family planning.
I was in Nairobi, Kenya, this summer, along with some other Members and the Minister responsible for the Status of Women (Mr. McLean). I can tell the House that the number one issue in Third World countries is that of over-population and family planning. We have to deal with this constructively, both internationally and here at home.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT RESPECTING LEGAL COUNSEL FOR UNBORN CHILD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by commending the Hon. Member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. O'Neil) for the Bill he has placed before us today. It was a new concept for me when I first read it, yet I think it has real merit. I would like to see the Bill go to committee so that we could discuss it more fully. We could call witnesses and fully deal with this concept and the issue of abortion itself. I would also commend the Hon. Member for London East (Mr. Jepson) for his comments. I think they were very well expressed and well taken.
The Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) said that she did not like the fact every three or four weeks she had to get up to respond to something like this, to in essence say no to the request being made by a Member. The fact that it is coming up so often is very significant. I encourage the Hon. Member to do what she would do on many other topics. If we constantly raise the question, say, of pensions or family allow-
Criminal Code
ances, she would certainly like us to look at that very seriously. Well, here is an issue which keeps coming up. Let us address it equally seriously and make sure we can take this Bill to committee and fully investigate all the facts surrounding the Bill. I ask for a little consistency from the Member in the way in which she addresses this Bill. Rather than complaining that the issue keeps coming up so often, let us deal with the fact that it does and start addressing it properly.
As I said, this Bill represents a novel concept where we would have someone present at an abortion committee hearing who would speak for the unborn. That is an excellent concept. I am not sure how it would work in our abortion clinics across the land. It is my understanding that abortion clinics do not have these therapeutic committees, but that is something we could deal with in our committee. I still believe we should take it to committee to be explored. It is an excellent concept which we should examine.
If I recall correctly, the Member for Vancouver East said that we should not force on others our morality and views about some of the issues which we as individuals hold very dear. While I can understand some of her argument, I have studied this topic at length. I was a member of a hospital board for several years in Kitchener-Waterloo. I recall that when we studied this topic at the Kitchener-Waterloo hospital board we spent over a year using the medical expertise that was available to us. In spite of the fact that we were only carrying out about 40 per cent to 50 per cent of the abortion requests coming to the hospital, and therefore taking quite a narrow application of the law, we found that our therapeutic abortion committee was approving abortions for 66 different reasons under the present law. I suggest that it was far too liberal an interpretation of the law.
We must take seriously the argument not to force our morality on others. Therefore, when it comes to the topic of abortion I suggest that we should be as thorough and objective as possible. Rather than talking about the side issues that surround this topic, and becoming involved in all the emotions that come into play, let us address the central issue: Are we dealing with a human being who should have the full protection of the law or are we not? If we are dealing with a human being, let us ensure that they have the full protection of the law. If not, let us withdraw this section from the Criminal Code and let people simply do what they wish. We must be as objective as we can.
I am particularly interested in the fact that in 1975 in West Germany the Lower House was asked to deal with that country's abortion law. Its practice is quite similar to ours today. It was cognizant of the fact that from 1933 to 1945 Germany had denied human rights to a certain segment of its population. It wanted to be very careful that it was truly a full democratic state in the true sense of the word, giving full protection of the law to all its citizens, including the unborn if that foetus was considered a person. Therefore, the question was given to the Supreme Court which called in 133 world

January 17, 1986
Criminal Code
experts, including geneticists, obstetricians and gynaecologists. They were asked to address this question of whether or not a foetus is a human being and therefore should be accorded the full and equal protection of the law. After two weeks of considering this question this group brought in a unanimous recommendation. In answer to the question: "When does the foetus gain the civil right to life?", they answered:
Life, in the sense of historical existence of a human individual, exists according to definite biological-physiological knowledge, in any case, from the fourteenth day after conception.
The reason they chose the fourteenth day after conception is that it is possible for the cells to divide into twins or triplets up to that point.
Their statement is remarkable because it was unanimous and specific in stating that life exists from the fourteenth day because the cells could divide into twins or triplets before that time. We should also note that this recognition of life is even before the woman knows that she is pregnant. Therefore, according to these 133 world experts, we are dealing with a human being.
I submit that if that is the evidence and we are trying to be as objective as we can, as we must, then our actions should begin to follow the facts. We would be required to do so in economic policy and we are surely required to do so in all of our social policy. Let us begin being honest about abortion policy. The abortion statistics in this country today are a travesty of justice. It is a pure refusal of people to address the facts because they do not want to be bothered. They have already made up their mind.
The House will know that Dr. Morgentaler opened a clinic in Toronto. This was challenged in the courts and he was acquitted. The Government of Ontario appealed and the acquittal was overturned. Now he is permitted to continue with his clinic in spite of that. The existence of the clinic is against the law which specifically states that abortions much be dealt with by a therapeutic abortion committee in the hospitals. Even Grade 3 children could understand that. However, we sit here in our comfortable seats and ignore that fact as if it does not matter. It is a sad commentary on Members and a sad commentary on our society.
Let us begin to be objective. This Bill asks that we at least have someone present to speak for that child. Surely that is a minimum request. This Bill is attempting to have us think and become objective again in order to be truly supportive of the weaker in our society who need the full protection of the law. The strong will look after themselves. The rich will look after themselves. Let us begin defending those who cannot defend themselves.
I urge Members to seriously think about what we are doing and pass this Bill to committee so that we can have an objective, fair and calm discussion, not addressing all the side issues but the real issue about the protection of the unborn.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT RESPECTING LEGAL COUNSEL FOR UNBORN CHILD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 also welcome the opportunity to speak to this Bill introduced by my seatmate, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton Highlands-Can-so (Mr. O'Neil). The Bill before us today proposes that the unborn child be represented by legal counsel for the purposes of the therapeutic abortion committee meetings pursuant to the provisions of the Criminal Code. This would be a fundamental and welcome change to the present procedures and I would also like to see this Bill go to committee.
Today we are focusing our attention once again on a very important moral issue. In 1969, the Criminal Code was amended to provide that an abortion could lawfully be performed by a qualified medical practitioner in an accredited or approved hospital if the therapeutic abortion committee of the hospital has issued a certificate stating that in its opinion the continuation of the pregnancy would or would be likely to endanger the woman's life or health. However, the life and health of the mother are very rarely, if ever, endangered.
Many doctors are signing death warrants instead and many so-called doctors, such as Dr. Morgentaler mentioned by the Hon. Member for Kitchener (Mr. Reimer), are performing abortions in non-approved locations. This situation should be investigated. Furthermore, in some provinces the federal law is not obeyed at all. In some locations the abortions are outnumbering the live births.
In 1979, the federal Government appointed the committee on the operation of the abortion law to conduct a fact-finding study to determine whether the procedure provided in the Criminal Code for obtaining therapeutic abortions was operating equitably across Canada. This group, under the chairmanship of Robin Badgley of the University of Toronto included as other members of the committee, Dr. Marian G. Powell of the Toronto General Hospital and Montreal lawyer, Madame Denise Fortin-Caron. The committee was not asked to consider the merits of the abortion law itself or to make recommendations but I believe this should have been done at the time.
Earlier, I spoke to a Bill similar to this one. With modern technology such as imaging created by ultrasound vibrations, new medical evidence has emerged and has proven that life exists since conception.
